Predicted LowAT occured in 57.1% of aOVS and in 30.3% of OVS. OVS showed greater nocturnal hypoxemia and respiratory events, whereas aOVS showed more frequently recorded awakenings, insomnia symptoms and fatigue. The trend emerging from the differing prevalence of predicted LowAT appears interesting but is currently exploratory. Future prospective studies involving large cohorts will be needed to verify the true prevalence of LowAT in these two populations.

papers.title: Gray matter alterations and their atlas-based spatial associations with neurotransmitter distributions in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder.
papers.abstract: Multiple neurotransmitter systems are implicated in the pathophysiology of isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) and its progression to α-synucleinopathy. This study aimed to identify baseline gray matter (GM) alterations in patients with iRBD compared with healthy controls and to examine their spatial correspondence with known neurotransmitter distributions. We further characterized GM patterns associated with future phenoconversion and their neurochemical context. A total of 109 patients with iRBD who completed at least one follow-up evaluation and 24 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging. Gray matter volume (GMV) alterations were assessed using the CAT12 toolbox. Spatial correlations between group-level GMV difference maps and neurotransmitter atlases were evaluated using the JuSpace toolbox. At baseline, patients with iRBD showed reduced GMV in the right cerebellar cortex and vermis, along with increased GMV in the left putamen and pallidum. These GMV alterations demonstrated significant spatial correspondence with dopaminergic receptor and transporter maps, including dopamine D2 receptors and the dopamine transporter (DAT). Among patients with iRBD, those who subsequently phenoconverted exhibited lower baseline GMV in the right medial orbital gyrus compared with non-converters. This pattern showed significant spatial correlations with serotonergic (5-HT2A), glutamatergic (mGluR5), GABAergic (GABAa), and dopaminergic (FDOPA) neurotransmitter maps. Patients with iRBD exhibit distinct patterns of GMV alteration that spatially align with dopaminergic neurotransmitter distribution maps, while phenoconversion is associated with GM changes corresponding to multiple neurotransmitter systems, although the phenoconversion findings are exploratory.

papers.title: Impaired brain reserve is associated with increased risk of overt hepatic encephalopathy occurrence in patients with cirrhosis.
papers.abstract: Overt hepatic encephalopathy (OHE) is a severe complication of liver cirrhosis, independently associated with a poor outcome and subsequent cognitive impairment, which are often, but not always, related to covert hepatic encephalopathy (CHE). Brain reserve, reflecting overall brain health, may be reduced in patients with cirrhosis because liver disease and brain disorders share several risk factors. Patients with impaired brain reserve may display cognitive impairments that differ from those observed in CHE. We hypothesize that brain reserve could influence OHE occurrence. Retrospective study of a prospective cohort of outpatients with cirrhosis (from March 2018 to June 2024) referred for cognitive complaints, generally in the setting of a pre-TIPS or pre-transplant evaluation. A multimodal evaluation was conducted, including a clinical evaluation, blood sampling including ammonia level, complete neuropsychological testing, electroencephalogram (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging with spectroscopy (MRS). The diagnosis of CHE was established by an adjudication committee based on this multimodal evaluation. History of OHE (HOHE) was collected retrospectively, and OHE occurrence was assessed prospectively. A total of 164 patients were included. The median age was 62 years [55-67], 72% were male, risk factors for cirrhosis were alcohol/ metabolic factors/viral for 65/52/14% of them. Median MELD was 12 [9-15] and Child Pugh index 8 [6-9]. Overall, 67% had a history of OHE and 66% were diagnosed with CHE according to the adjudication committee. Patients with HOHE displayed more brain atrophy at MRI (p = 0.045). During the one-year follow-up, a total of 48 patients developed OHE. In multivariate Fine and Gray competing risk analysis, brain atrophy (sHR = 4.80 [1.31 - 17.60], p = 0.018) and impaired memory evaluated by the FCSRT (sHR = 0.86 [0.79 - 0.94], p < 0.001) were independently associated with OHE occurrence, alongside with HOHE (sHR = 3.37 [1.14 - 9.99], p = 0.028), baseline MELD score (sHR = 1.21 [1.09 - 1.34], p < 0.001), EEG Background rhythm (sHR = 0.71 [0.50 - 1.00], p = 0.048) but not ammonia level (p = 0.057). Memory impairment and brain atrophy, which reflect an impaired brain reserve, are independently associated with OHE occurrence in patients with cirrhosis for CHE suspicion. Our results suggest that an impaired brain reserve is associated with increased risk of OHE occurrence in patients with cirrhosis.

papers.title: Chronic non-24-h light-dark cycles alter healthspan measures but not overall survival in male C57BL/6 J mice.
papers.abstract: Circadian biology is recognized for its importance to physiology and metabolism, with implications for healthy aging and disease risk. To test whether altering the number of imposed environmental cycles experienced per unit chronological time affects health biomarkers and lifespan, we compressed and expanded the photic cycle (T-cycle, combined light:dark length) by ~ 10% relative to the 24-h day. Male C57BL/6 J mice (n = 60 per group, 12 weeks old) were randomized to one of three T-cycles: T ~ 22-, T = 24-, or T ~ 26-h. Seasonal variations in light:dark proportions of the photoperiod from 8:16 to 16:8 and back over 365 imposed photic cycles were applied to the T = 24 condition and scaled (+ / - 10%) for each. Body weight and food intake were measured weekly under ad libitum feeding, with body composition, metabolic rate, and functional measures collected. Mortality was measured daily, and survival was compared by Cox and linear mixed models (LMM). T-cycle group differences for health biomarkers were assessed with LMM. Mice gained weight early in life across all three T-cycles, with significant effects of time, T-cycle, and time*T-cycle interactions (p < 0.001, p < 0.001, p < 0.001; T ~ 22 quicker weight gain). Similar results were found for fat mass and lean mass, where significant (p < 0.05) time, T-cycle, and time*T-cycle interactions were observed. There was no significant difference among T-cycles for overall survival, mean longevity, or maximum lifespan (p = 0.086, p = 0.079, and p = 0.527, respectively). Mice experiencing 10% chronic contraction or extension of the daily T-cycle do not show significant differences in mortality versus the 24-h T-cycle controls.

papers.title: Subcutaneous apomorphine and the nonmotor features of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a heterogeneous, progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which nonmotor manifestations (autonomic, sleep-related, neuropsychiatric, and sensory) constitute integral components of the disease continuum, exerting a disproportionate influence on quality of life, long-term disability, and caregiver burden. These features comprise both persistent components intrinsic to neurodegeneration and state-dependent fluctuations mechanistically linked to the oscillating dopaminergic tone imposed by pulsatile oral therapy. Apomorphine occupies a singular pharmacological position among the PD armamentarium, distinguished by a receptor binding profile, physicochemical properties, and pharmacokinetics that set it apart from other dopamine agonists and from levodopa-based therapies. Nearly four decades of clinical experience have established its efficacy in attenuating motor fluctuations and dyskinesias via continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSAI). Its effects on the nonmotor dimension of PD remain however incompletely characterized, reflecting both limited research investment and methodological constraints inherent to nonmotor outcome assessment and to apomorphine therapy itself. This narrative review and expert opinion examines the pharmacological basis for apomorphine's putative nonmotor efficacy, clinical evidence across individual nonmotor domains and iatrogenic considerations before reassessing apomorphine's therapeutic positioning within the device-aided therapy landscape. Nonmotor features should be regarded as primary determinants of treatment decision-making rather than secondary endpoints. The emerging concept of "fluctuation-dominant" PD provides a framework in which nonmotor fluctuation burden alone may constitute sufficient indication for CSAI, with direct implications for patient selection, timing of initiation, and redefinition of therapeutic goals beyond motor control.

papers.title: Ru-SATED 4.0: a clean start for measuring sleep health.
Human Sleep Project (HSP): Is an Era of Big Data Coming in Clinical Sleep Medicine?
LOW-FLOW NOCTURNAL OXYGEN THERAPY FOR THE TREATMENT OF CENTRAL SLEEP APNEA IN CHRONIC HEART FAILURE: THE PAST, the PRESENT, and the FUTURE.
papers.abstract: Central sleep apnea (CSA), commonly seen in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fractions (HFrEF), is associated with hypoxia, heightened sympathetic activity, and poor clinical outcomes. While several CSA therapies reduce the apnea-hypopnea index, none have been shown to improve long-term important clinical outcomes. Nocturnal oxygen therapy (NOT) represents a physiologically sound approach to the treatment of CSA. Evidence supports the potential benefits of NOT in such patients, but no proof of its effectiveness on hard outcomes exists. Thus, there has been a longstanding need for a randomized controlled trial of NOT for CSA in HFrEF patients. The ideal trial would establish the rationale for NOT by measuring clinically meaningful outcomes, use rigorous methodologies such as double-blinding and a sham control, and optimize safety by delivering oxygen at doses that ameliorate hypoxemia and avoid hyperoxia. Such a trial (LOFT-HF NCT03745898) was indeed eventually sponsored by the National Institute of Heath and was initiated in 2018-2019. However, the trial was halted during the COVID-19 pandemic due to slow enrollment. Findings were recently published and did not provide a firm conclusion but suggested potential harm in the NOT arm based on a very small number of participants. Meanwhile, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) published recently new treatment guidelines for CSA, suggesting use NOT in CSA. In this article, we attempt to reconcile the LOFT-HF trial findings with existing literature and the new AASM CSA management guidelines and discuss future research needs.

papers.title: Topical Ketoprofen 5%, Amitriptyline HCL 5%, and Lidocaine 5% Compounded in VersaPro Cream for Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Peripheral neuropathy is a common complication of type 1 and type 2 diabetes, often resulting in severe pain that significantly impacts the quality of life. This case report describes the treatment of a 56-year-old female patient with severe peripheral neuropathic pain in the lower extremities due to type 1 diabetes after pain persisted while using conventional therapy. The patient was prescribed a compounded topical cream containing Ketoprofen 5%, Amitriptyline HCL 5%, and Lidocaine 5% in VersaPro Cream Base to help address symptoms of diabetic peripheral neuropathy in addition to her systemic medications. Over an 8-week treatment period, the patient reported significant reductions in pain intensity and improved functional outcomes, including sleep quality and mobility. This case highlights the potential benefit of compounded topical analgesics as an adjunct therapy for managing neuropathic pain in patients with limited treatment options, and when conventional options may not be suitable.

papers.title: The Cutaneous Melatoninergic System: Endogenous Biology and Potential for Therapeutic Targeting.
papers.abstract: Melatonin is best known as a pineal hormone that regulates circadian rhythms, but the skin also possesses an intrinsic melatoninergic system capable of local synthesis, metabolism and signalling. This system encompasses classical melatonin receptors, biologically active metabolites, non-classical signalling pathways and receptor-independent intracellular actions involved in cutaneous stress responses, with emerging evidence for broader roles in skin homeostasis. In this review, we integrate current mechanistic and clinical evidence on the cutaneous melatoninergic system and critically examine its therapeutic relevance. Human evidence is most consistent for the photoprotective effects of topical melatonin, whereas clinical data for photoaging, radiation dermatitis, wound healing, hair disorders, inflammatory dermatoses, pigmentary disorders and chronic pruritus remain limited or preliminary. Interpretation is further constrained by small sample sizes, heterogeneous formulations, short follow-up and frequent use of combination products. Importantly, the clinical efficacy of exogenous melatonin and evidence that the endogenous cutaneous melatoninergic system represents a disease-modifying therapeutic target are distinct questions. Establishing the therapeutic relevance of the endogenous system will require characterisation of disease-associated alterations in local melatonin synthesis, metabolism and signalling, demonstration of molecular target engagement, and linkage to clinically meaningful outcomes.

papers.title: Cortical traveling wave analysis reveals weaker resting forward theta waves and greater task-related modulation in obsessive compulsive disorder.
papers.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is associated with abnormalities in large-scale brain network dynamics. Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) captures local oscillatory activity but does not characterize spatiotemporal propagation patterns. This study investigates cortical traveling waves, which index directional information flow across the cortex, to determine whether they provide novel insights into altered neural communication in OCD. Resting-state (eyes-closed) and task-based (Go/NoGo, Flanker) EEG were recorded from 25 individuals with OCD and 27 healthy controls (HCs). Traveling waves were quantified along midline electrodes using two-dimensional Fast Fourier Transforms to extract forward (posterior-to-anterior) and backward (anterior-to-posterior) propagation in theta (4-8Hz) and alpha (8-13Hz) bands. Group differences were assessed using Bayesian and frequentist linear mixed-effects models controlling for age and sex. At rest, a significant group-by-direction interaction was observed in the theta band (P = 0.0006), driven by weaker forward traveling wave strength in OCD relative to HC. No group differences were observed for backward waves or in the alpha band. During the Flanker task, the OCD group showed a significantly greater increase in forward theta wave strength from rest than HC (P = 0.022). No associations were found between traveling wave measures and symptom severity. OCD is characterized by altered theta-band traveling wave dynamics, specifically reduced forward (bottom-up) signaling at rest, and increased task-related modulation during the Flanker task. These findings suggest disrupted hierarchical cortical communication and inefficient engagement of sensory-driven processes. The absence of symptom correlations suggests a potential trait-like neurophysiological marker or endophenotype of OCD.

papers.title: Adjunctive Trazodone Effects on Sleep, Mood, and Circulating 5-HT and BDNF in Depression.
papers.abstract: This retrospective study evaluated the association of adjunctive trazodone with sleep architecture, sleep quality, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and circulating 5-HT and BDNF levels in patients with depression. A total of 156 propensity-score-matched patients were included in the final analysis, including 78 who received conventional antidepressant therapy (fluvoxamine monotherapy; control group) and 78 who received combined trazodone and fluvoxamine therapy (observation group). Both treatment regimens were continued for 8 consecutive weeks. Propensity score matching (PSM) was used to balance baseline characteristics between the groups. Sleep architecture, sleep quality, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and circulating 5-HT and BDNF levels were assessed at the prespecified clinical time points. Compared with the control group, the observation group demonstrated significantly reduced awake time, prolonged rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and slow-wave sleep (SWS) duration, improved sleep quality, and lower depression and anxiety scores at week 4 (HAMD: 8.23 ± 1.25 vs. 11.88 ± 2.50; HAMA: 4.35 ± 1.32 vs. 7.89 ± 2.17; both P < 0.001), together with higher circulating 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels at week 8. Furthermore, the overall clinical response rate was significantly higher in the observation group than in the control group. These findings suggest that adjunctive trazodone was associated with better sleep-related and clinical outcomes, as well as higher circulating 5-HT and BDNF levels, than fluvoxamine monotherapy.

papers.title: Association Between Dietary Vitamin Intake and Short Sleep Duration Among Adults in the United States: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) Data.
papers.abstract: Objective Short sleep duration (SSD) and inadequate dietary vitamin intake are both relevant to overall health and may share relationships with chronic disease risk. However, the relationship between dietary vitamin intake and sleep duration remains incompletely characterized, particularly when vitamin intake is evaluated relative to total energy consumption; additionally, limited research has been done to evaluate the relationship between SSD and vitamins that are not traditionally associated with sleep. Understanding these associations may help clarify potential nutritional factors related to sleep duration. This study evaluated associations between SSD and dietary intake of vitamins A, B1, B2, B3, B6, B9, B12, C, D, E, and K per 1,000 kilocalories among adults in the United States. Materials and methods This cross-sectional study used 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data. Adults aged ≥20 years with complete sleep, dietary, covariate, and Day 1 dietary weight data were included (n=4,169). SSD was defined as fewer than 7 hours of usual weekday/workday sleep. Primary endpoints were vitamins A, B6, and K; all other vitamins were secondary endpoints. Participants were categorized into low, middle, and high intake tertiles for each vitamin. Separate weighted logistic regression models were performed using the NHANES Day 1 dietary sample weight and adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, income-to-poverty ratio, total energy intake, and body mass index. NHANES strata and primary sampling units were not incorporated into the analysis. Results SSD prevalence decreased across low-to-high intake groups for vitamin A (24.2% to 16.4%), vitamin B6 (22.7% to 18.7%), and vitamin K (23.5% to 17.8%). Higher intake remained associated with lower odds of SSD for vitamin A (aOR=0.710, 95% CI 0.710-0.711), vitamin B6 (aOR=0.724, 95% CI 0.723-0.725), and vitamin K (aOR=0.815, 95% CI 0.814-0.816). Weaker inverse associations were observed for vitamins B1, B2, B3, B12, D, and E. Vitamin C demonstrated a nonlinear inverse pattern, whereas vitamin B9 showed a direct association. Conclusion Higher dietary intake of vitamins A, B6, and K was associated with lower odds of SSD among adults in the United States. Causation cannot be inferred because of the cross-sectional study design. In addition, confidence intervals and significance estimates should be interpreted cautiously because NHANES strata and primary sampling units were not incorporated into the analysis. Prospective studies using full complex survey methods are warranted to further evaluate these associations.

papers.title: Individual-level quality-of-life changes are common after aneurysm screening in women: A prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Screening for intracranial aneurysms enables the treatment of lesions at risk of rupture, but concerns remain about its psychological effects. We investigated the impact of screening on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in 50-60-year-old female smokers. How does aneurysm screening affect HRQoL? HRQoL was prospectively assessed using 15D and EQ-5D-3L before, 3 months, and 12 months after screening. Changes in individual HRQoL domains were analyzed, and MIC thresholds were used to define clinically relevant changes in the EQ index and EQ visual analogue scale (EQ VAS). Linear mixed models determined whether the timepoint, computed tomography angiography (CTA) results, or their interaction affected EQ outcomes. Of 108 women, 13 had abnormal vascular findings, and two underwent surgery. Three-month follow-up questionnaires were returned by 92 participants and 57 completed the 12-month follow-up. Linear mixed models showed no effect of timepoint, CTA results, or their interaction on EQ index or EQ VAS. Nevertheless, 54 participants (59%) deteriorated in at least one 15D domain, including depression (n = 14), sleep (n = 12), and anxiety (n = 9). Sixty-seven reported improvements, notably in sleep (n = 22), symptoms and discomfort (n = 19), and vitality (n = 19). By MIC thresholds, 11 participants showed clinically significant EQ index worsening and nine improvement. Overall EQ-5D scores suggested no HRQoL impairment, but individual-level analyses revealed worsening of anxiety and depression irrespective of screening results. Standard HRQoL instruments may miss psychosocial effects of screening. Future studies should incorporate pre-invitation baseline assessments and anxiety-specific measures alongside generic HRQoL questionnaires.

papers.title: Decoding Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of qEEG biomarkers across clinical domains.
papers.abstract: This systematic review synthesized evidence on quantitative EEG (qEEG) correlates of Parkinson's disease (PD) across five domains: cognition, motor function, pharmacological interventions, neuromodulation, and sleep/non-motor features, evaluating qEEG's potential as a biomarker across these clinical domains. Following PRISMA, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus for studies published from 1991 to 2025. We included studies with ≥10 idiopathic PD patients, resting-state qEEG, and empirical data. Methodological quality was assessed using JBI checklists and AMSTAR. We included 89 studies. Spectral slowing - reduced posterior dominant frequency and increased theta power - was the most consistent correlate of cognitive impairment. Connectivity measures (PLV, graph metrics) showed stronger associations with motor dysfunction, gait impairment, and freezing than spectral power alone. qEEG changed with dopaminergic drugs (increased alpha/beta) and neuromodulation (DBS, tDCS, rTMS, neurofeedback). Sleep studies revealed spindle density reductions linked to dementia risk. qEEG is a promising biomarker for PD, with distinct electrophysiological correlates across cognitive, motor, pharmacological, and neuromodulatory domains. However, methodological standardization is needed before clinical use. With standardized protocols and multicenter validation, qEEG could aid diagnosis, progression tracking, and personalized therapy in PD.

papers.title: Effectiveness Evaluation and Predictive Model Construction of Multi-modal Intervention Program Based on Psychological Resilience Theory in Perioperative Anxiety Management for Cataract Surgery.
papers.abstract: To investigate the effectiveness of a multi-modal intervention program based on psychological resilience theory in perioperative anxiety management for cataract surgery and to establish an anxiety risk prediction model. A prospective randomized controlled trial was conducted, including 120 patients who underwent phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation in the ophthalmology department of the hospital from March 2024 to March 2025. Participants were randomly assigned to an intervention group (n=63) and a control group (n=57). The control group received routine perioperative care, while the intervention group received a psychological resilience theory-based intervention program in addition to routine care. The primary outcome measure was the change in State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) state anxiety scores. Secondary outcome measures included Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC-25) scores, Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-7) scores, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), physiological indicators (blood pressure, heart rate), Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores, surgical cooperation scores, and postoperative complication rates. Multiple stepwise regression analysis was used to construct an anxiety risk prediction model, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was employed to evaluate the model's predictive performance. No statistically significant differences were found in baseline characteristics between the 2 groups (all P > .05). The intervention group demonstrated significantly greater reductions in STAI state anxiety scores compared to the control group at all follow-up time points. At 1 month postoperatively, the intervention group achieved a mean reduction of 16.6 ± 8.9 points compared to 9.6 ± 7.2 points in the control group (mean difference=7.0, 95% CI: 3.9-10.1, P < .001). The intervention group showed significantly greater improvements in CD-RISC-25 scores at 1-month follow-up compared to the control group (mean increase: 16.1 ± 9.8 vs. 3.6 ± 8.2 points, P < .001). The GAD-7 and PSQI scores showed significantly greater reductions in the intervention group at all postoperative time points (all P < .001). At 30 minutes preoperatively, the intervention group showed significantly lower systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and heart rate compared to the control group (127.8 ± 13.2 vs. 137.4 ± 16.1 mmHg, 77.9 ± 9.4 vs. 84.2 ± 11.3 mmHg, 74.2 ± 10.8 vs. 86.7 ± 13.4 beats/min, respectively, all P ≤ .001). The intervention group demonstrated significantly lower VAS pain scores at all postoperative time points, higher surgical cooperation scores (4.3 ± 0.8 vs. 3.6 ± 0.9, P < .001), shorter time to first ambulation (7.2 ± 2.4 vs. 9.8 ± 3.1 hours, P < .001), and reduced length of stay (2.3 ± 0.7 vs. 2.9 ± 0.9 days, P < .001). The total incidence of postoperative complications was significantly lower in the intervention group compared to the control group (28.6% vs. 56.1%, P=.003). The constructed anxiety risk prediction model included 7 predictive factors: age, gender, education level, previous surgical history, baseline blood pressure, baseline psychological resilience level, and social support score. The model demonstrated good fit (R 2=0.689, adjusted R 2=0.671), with an area under the ROC curve of 0.863 (95% CI: 0.802-0.924), sensitivity of 84.2%, and specificity of 81.4%. The multi-modal intervention program based on psychological resilience theory effectively reduces perioperative anxiety levels in cataract patients, enhances psychological resilience, improves physiological indicators, alleviates postoperative pain, increases surgical cooperation, shortens recovery time, and reduces complication rates. The constructed anxiety risk prediction model demonstrates good predictive performance.

papers.title: Cerebellar Topological Alterations Across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum.
papers.abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized as a network disconnection syndrome. Despite evidence implicating the cerebellum in cognitive network integration, its associated electrophysiological network topology dynamics across the AD continuum remain unexplored. Methods: We enrolled 34 healthy controls (HC), 40 patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 30 AD patients in this study. Cortical and cerebellar signals were recorded with a whole-brain EEG cap, and weighted functional connectivity networks were constructed using the phase-locking value (PLV). Graph theory was used to analyze network topological metrics across the AD continuum, focusing on cerebellar nodes. Topological metrics were correlated with neuropsychological scores, and network-based statistics (NBS) identified differential connectivity patterns among groups. Results: Network changes were most prominent in the theta band, with additional alterations in the delta band. Both MCI and AD groups showed reduced small-world metrics, although small-world organization remained present. These groups also showed increased nodal centrality in the frontal, occipital and cerebellar regions (at CB1, CB2 and CBZ in MCI but only at CBZ in AD) but decreased in the central and temporal regions. NBS analysis identified selective theta-band reorganization of cerebello-cortical connectivity. An inverted U-shaped relationship was found between cerebellar nodal centrality and neuropsychological scale scores. Conclusions: The cerebellar theta rhythm may be a key pattern involved in cognitive processing, and the topological changes of the cortical-cerebellar network may represent candidate electrophysiological network markers across different AD stages. These markers may reflect stage-related differences in cerebellar function, shifting from compensation in MCI to decompensation in AD.

papers.title: Lamotrigine as a Potential Therapeutic Agent for Psychosomatic Disorders: Insights from a Drug Target-Based Mendelian Randomization Study.
papers.abstract: Several observational studies have identified mood disorders as a risk factor for psychosomatic disorders, and mood stabilizers like lamotrigine are hypothesized to have disease-modifying effects. This Mendelian randomization (MR) study aimed to 1) investigate the causal association between mood disorders and 4 psychosomatic disorders (diabetes, hypertension, sleep duration disorder, thyroid problems) and 2) evaluate the potential impact of 14 drug targets of lamotrigine on these psychosomatic disorders. Fourteen lamotrigine drug targets (CACNA1E, SCN11A, ADORA1, ADORA2A, ADRA1A, ADRA2A, ADRB1, DRD2, HRH1, OPRK1, CHRNA1, HTR2A, HTR3A, GRIA1) and 4 psychosomatic disorders were included. Two-sample MR analysis (primary: inverse variance weighted method) with sensitivity tests (MR-Egger, weighted median, MR-PRESSO) was conducted using public summary-level data (e.g., UK Biobank mood swings dataset: 325 480 European-ancestry individuals; DIAGRAM diabetes dataset: ~900 000 participants). Summary data-based MR (SMR) explored target gene expression-psychosomatic disorder links, and Bayesian colocalization verified result robustness. Only the lamotrigine target DRD2 showed significant associations with 3 psychosomatic disorders: hypertension (OR=1.23, 95% CI=1.09-1.39, P=1.34×10-5) and sleep disorders (OR=2.45, 95% CI=1.67-3.61, P=4.89×10-6), with consistent results in the validation dataset. In the validation dataset, DRD2 showed only a nominal association with diabetes (IVW OR=3.59; 95% CI, 1.15-11.23; P=.02), which did not meet the Bonferroni-corrected threshold. While primary MR analysis suggested an association between the lamotrigine target DRD2 and diabetes, hypertension, or sleep duration disorder, this was not validated by SMR or colocalization. Thus, lamotrigine's direct impact on these psychosomatic disorders remains unconfirmed, and cautious interpretation is needed for its potential off-label use in comorbid physical conditions. These findings highlight the value of multi-method genetic analyses to validate MR results and guide future clinical research.

papers.title: Physician documented fatigue among adults and children with inflammatory bowel disease: a nationwide routinely collected health data study from the epi-IIRN.
papers.abstract: We aimed to assess the rates of physician-documented fatigue according to diagnostic codes among patients with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) in a nationwide cohort and to identify clinical factors associated with its documentation. We used the nationwide epi- Israeli IBD Research Nucleus cohort derived from 4 HMOs covering approximately 98% of the Israeli population, matched to non-IBD controls. Physician-documented fatigue was defined using routinely collected ICD9 and textual codes and explored in association with demographic, laboratory-derived disease severity clusters, comorbidities, medications, healthcare utilization, and sickness absence. Predictors for fatigue documentation were explored using multivariable Cox models incorporating time-varying covariates. Fatigue was documented in 16.4% of the 31 945 patients with IBD and 11.0% of the 73 106 matched controls (odds ratio [OR] = 1.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.54-1.66). Fatigue was more prevalent in IBD than matched controls across age groups and comorbidity strata. Among patients with IBD, there was no difference in fatigue rate between those with Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Time-to-fatigue was shorter among females (P < .001). Across adult males and females and pediatric boys and girls, anemia, anxiety, and ≥3 healthcare contacts were independently associated with higher rates of fatigue documentation, with the strongest associations observed for frequent healthcare contact (HRs ranging from 4.21 [95% CI 1.49-11.70] to 10.22 [95% CI 7.47-13.90]). Longer disease duration was consistently associated with a lower hazard, while additional subgroup-specific associations were observed for sleep disorders, steroid dependency, and IBD-related medications. Fatigue is more frequently documented among patients with IBD than matched non-IBD controls, especially in females. Several risk factors were associated with fatigue which should be considered in clinical practice. The lower frequency of documented fatigue compared with patient-reported estimates suggests that routine clinical coding captures only part of the overall fatigue burden.

papers.title: Analysis of the Influencing Factors of Sleep Quality in Patients with Bipolar Disorder.
papers.abstract: To observe the sleep quality of patients with bipolar disorder (BD), analyze the possible causes of sleep disorders, and take targeted interventions, which are particularly necessary to improve the sleep quality of patients and promote the development of the disease. Between January 2022 and January 2024, 60 patients with BD were enrolled in the study, and sleep quality in all participants was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). By comparing the general data of patients with and without sleep disorders, the influencing factors that may lead to poor sleep quality were analyzed. The assessment results of the PSQI scale of 60 patients with BD showed that there were 40 patients with sleep disorders, which were included in the poor sleep quality group (PSQI ≥7); the average score of the PSQI scale was (15.25 ± 1.03) points. There were 20 patients without sleep disorders who were included in the good sleep quality group; the average score of PSQI scale was (3.20 ± 0.41) points. The Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), cortisol level and percentages of social support (low level), and coping style (negative coping) in the patients of poor sleep quality group were higher than those in the good sleep quality group (P < .05). Logistic regression analysis indicated that SAS, SDS, cortisol level, social support (low level), and coping style (negative coping) were all the factors that affected the sleep disorders in patients with BD (OR > 1, P = .017, .006, .014, .007, .005 respectively). Anxiety, depression, cortisol level, social support, and coping style are all related to the sleep quality of patients with BD. The SAS, SDS, cortisol levels, low social support, and negative coping style are risk factors for poor sleep quality.

papers.title: Interbrain synchrony analysis for fNIRS: A signal processing primer.
papers.abstract: Interbrain synchrony (IBS), also referred to as interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), has become a central construct in social neuroscience and beyond. It describes the temporal alignment of neural activity across individuals and has been studied in a range of paradigms, including sequential interactions, shared-stimulus settings, and hyperscanning, that is, the simultaneous neuroimaging of two or more individuals during real-time interaction. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is increasingly used for such studies because it supports portable, naturalistic, face-to-face paradigms. A central goal in these experiments is to quantify IBS between interacting individuals. Wavelet transform coherence (WTC) has become the most widely used method for estimating IBS in fNIRS studies. However, its application involves several non-trivial signal-processing assumptions and time-frequency trade-offs that are often not explicitly addressed, making it difficult to apply and interpret the method consistently. Reliable estimation of IBS is crucial not only for experimental design but also for the interpretation and comparison of results within and across studies. Here, we aim to support this endeavor by providing a principled overview of the relevant signal-processing foundations. To enable researchers to make informed methodological choices, the paper first introduces key concepts in time-frequency analysis and clarifies their relation to WTC. These principles are then connected to the analysis of IBS in fNIRS datasets, with particular emphasis on the time-frequency constraints inherent to wavelet-based methods. Building on these foundations, we provide practical recommendations for experiment design, preprocessing, and frequency targeting. By making resolution limits and analysis assumptions explicit, this primer aims to support improved study planning and more consistent interpretation of IBS in the rapidly growing field of fNIRS-based investigations and beyond. Establishing a shared methodological foundation for IBS analysis is essential for advancing toward more rigorous, transparent, and reproducible measurement of interpersonal brain dynamics in naturalistic neuroscience.

papers.title: Prevalence and determinants of fasting-related dizziness and hypoglycemic symptoms among adults during Ramadan in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: A community-based cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Ramadan fasting involves prolonged abstinence from food and fluids and may lead to dizziness and hypoglycemic-type symptoms. Community-based data on these symptoms among adults in Riyadh are limited. To determine the prevalence of fasting-related dizziness and hypoglycemic symptoms and identify associated risk factors among adults in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among adults (≥18 years) who fasted during Ramadan. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire. A fasting-related symptomatic episode was defined as the presence of ≥2 symptoms during fasting hours (dizziness, tremor, sweating, palpitations, severe fatigue, or fainting). Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression. Among 498 participants (50.0% female; mean body mass index [BMI] 24.9 ± 4.8 kg/m2), 37.3% reported at least one fasting-related symptom and 20.1% experienced a symptomatic episode. Dizziness (21.3%), palpitations (17.1%), and severe fatigue (12.2%) were the most common symptoms. Independent risk factors included diabetes (adjusted odds ratios [AOR] 11.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 5.18-23.47), underweight BMI (AOR 4.40, 95% CI 1.03-18.71), anemia (AOR 3.01, 95% CI 1.17-7.70), sleep duration >8 h (AOR 2.85, 95% CI 1.02-7.91), hypertension (AOR 2.73, 95% CI 1.19-6.28), moderate caffeine intake (101-200 mg/day) (AOR 2.59, 95% CI 1.24-5.44), and age 25-34 years (AOR 2.51, 95% CI 1.04-6.10). One in five adults experienced fasting-related symptomatic episodes during Ramadan. Diabetes, hypertension, anemia, underweight BMI, prolonged sleep, and moderate caffeine intake were significant risk factors. These findings support pre-Ramadan risk assessment and targeted counseling to promote safer fasting practices.
papers.journal: Journal of family medicine and primary care

papers.title: Screen time exposure, sleep alterations, and their relationship with excess weight in children and adolescents.
papers.abstract: The digital era has led to an unprecedented increase in screen time exposure among youth, creating a critical intersection between technology use, sleep hygiene, and metabolic health. To evaluate the association between daily screen time, sleep quality, and the prevalence of overweight and obesity in a pediatric clinical population. A cross-sectional study was conducted on 70 patients (mean age 10.8 years). Subjects were categorized into obese (n = 44) and non-obese (n = 26) groups. Anthropometric data, body composition (perivisceral fat), biochemical parameters [insulin, Homeostasis Model Assessment (HOMA), lipid profile], and lifestyle habits (Krece Plus and KIDMED tests) were analyzed. Binary logistic regression was performed to estimate odds ratios (OR) for obesity and sleep disturbances. Obesity was significantly associated with higher perivisceral fat (P < 0.001), systolic blood pressure (P = 0.009), insulin levels (P = 0.035), and HOMA index (P = 0.024), alongside lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (P < 0.001). Sociodemographic analysis revealed that maternal education level was significantly lower in the obese group (P = 0.006). Regarding lifestyle, obese children reported significantly higher daily screen time (2.9 hours vs 2.1 hours; P = 0.047) and shorter sleep duration (8.4 hours vs 9.1 hours; P = 0.021). The prevalence of chronic sleep disturbances was notably higher in obese subjects (39% vs 8.3%; P = 0.016). After adjusting for confounders, screen time was strongly associated with a higher risk of obesity (OR: 3.08; 95%CI: 1.53-7.90) and sleep problems (OR: 1.65; 95%CI: 0.96-2.99). Excessive screen time and poor sleep quality are strongly associated with pediatric obesity and its metabolic comorbidities. Furthermore, lower maternal education level and family history of diabetes are significant compounding factors. Clinical interventions should address digital hygiene and sleep quality as essential pillars in the management of childhood excess weight.

papers.title: Food Insecurity and Academic Performance among Postsecondary Students: A Global Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Food insecurity is increasingly recognized as a significant public health concern among postsecondary students worldwide. Emerging evidence suggests that inadequate access to food may negatively affect academic success; however, the scope and consistency of this relationship have not been comprehensively synthesized. This scoping review aimed to systematically identify, map, and summarize the existing literature on the relationship between food insecurity and academic performance among postsecondary students worldwide. The review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. Six electronic databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and ERIC) were searched from inception to November 2025. Eligibility criteria were defined using the Population, Concept, Context framework. Data were extracted and synthesized descriptively. Of 3078 records identified, 86 studies met the inclusion criteria, including 67 quantitative studies, 11 qualitative studies, and 8 mixed-methods studies. Most studies were conducted in the United States (n = 69). Across study designs, food insecurity was consistently associated with poorer academic outcomes, including lower grade point average, reduced academic achievement, impaired concentration, lower class attendance and engagement, increased course withdrawal and failure, delayed graduation, and lower educational attainment. Several studies identified anxiety, depression, psychological undefined distress, sleep disturbances, and financial strain as potential mechanisms linking food insecurity to academic performance. Qualitative evidence highlighted students' experiences of hunger, fatigue, stress, competing financial demands, and work-study disagreement as barriers to academic success. The available evidence consistently indicates that food insecurity is associated with poorer academic performance among postsecondary students. Addressing food insecurity is a strategic opportunity to support student success, retention, and educational attainment. Additional longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to strengthen causal inference and identify effective approaches to improving both food security and academic outcomes in higher education settings.

papers.title: Environmental enrichment as a multisystem modulator of neurotransmitter function: mechanisms, plasticity, and therapeutic implications.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) has emerged as a powerful non-pharmacological strategy for reshaping brain function through experience dependent plasticity. By integrating sensory, cognitive, motor, and social stimulation, EE provides a biologically relevant framework for understanding how external environments influence neurotransmitter systems that govern mood, cognition, stress adaptation, and neurodegeneration. In this review, we examined the effects of EE on major neurotransmitter pathways, including serotonergic, dopaminergic, glutamatergic, GABAergic, cholinergic, adrenergic, and histaminergic systems. We conducted a structured narrative search of PubMed, supplemented by Google Scholar reference list searching and informed by PRISMA reporting principles. The literature search covered studies published through 4 September 2026. The initial search, completed in February 2025, included 136 articles. A supplemental update screened 108 PubMed records and identified seven additional eligible primary studies, resulting in an updated evidence synthesis comprising 143 articles. Across predominantly preclinical studies, EE was consistently associated with enhanced neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, stress resilience, and improved behavioral and cognitive outcomes, accompanied by neurotransmitter related changes across multiple brain systems. The most robust evidence supported modulation of serotonergic, dopaminergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic pathways, whereas adrenergic and histaminergic effects were less well characterized and often indirect. Mechanistically, these effects converged on altered receptor and transporter expression, neurotrophic signaling, CREB dependent transcriptional regulation, and epigenetic remodeling. Collectively, the evidence positions EE as a multisystem regulator of neurotransmitter function with potential relevance to mood disorders, neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, stroke, addiction, and cognitive decline. Nevertheless, the field remains limited by the predominance of animal data and by substantial heterogeneity in enrichment paradigms. Future translational and clinical studies are needed to define the most effective EE components, timing, and intensity for therapeutic application in humans.

papers.title: Unleashing children's potential: An evidence-based narrative review of strategies to enhance cognitive function and intelligence in school-age children.
papers.abstract: School-age cognitive development (6-12 years) represents a critical window of neural plasticity, during which intelligence and executive function can be meaningfully enhanced. Once considered largely fixed, these cognitive capacities are now recognized as dynamic, multifactorial, and modifiable through environmental, nutritional, educational, and psychosocial interventions. This review synthesizes current evidence on strategies to optimize cognitive function in typically developing children as well as special populations, including those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, learning disabilities, twice exceptional profiles, or socio-economic disadvantage. We examine the impact of macronutrient and micronutrient intake, gut-brain interactions, physical activity, sleep quality, parenting practices, stress regulation, educational curricula, digital learning tools, mindfulness, and social-emotional learning, highlighting mechanistic pathways, intervention effectiveness, and population-specific considerations. Methodological challenges, including heterogeneity, cultural bias, and translational gaps, are critically appraised. Finally, we propose priorities for multimodal, personalized, and scalable interventions, informed by perspectives from precision education, implementation science, and longitudinal research. By integrating neuroscientific, educational, and psychosocial insights, this review provides actionable recommendations for clinicians, educators, and policymakers to maximize children's cognitive potential, academic achievement, and long-term adaptive outcomes.

papers.title: Circadian rhythm dysregulation and ferroptosis in hypertension: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
papers.abstract: Hypertension exhibits a pronounced circadian rhythm; however, the mechanisms by which circadian disruption translates temporal imbalance into sustained vascular and renal injury remain unclear. Increasing evidence suggests that circadian misalignment may promote endothelial dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and renal injury through ferroptosis driven by oxidative stress dysregulation, thereby increasing the risk of hypertension. Based on current evidence, this review proposes that circadian disruption induces a temporal mismatch between oxidative stress generation and antioxidant defense, thereby lowering the threshold for ferroptosis in cardiovascular and renal tissues. This process may amplify hemodynamic stress, impair endothelial integrity, and disturb renal sodium handling, ultimately contributing to the development and progression of hypertension. Although direct causal evidence remains limited, this review integrates circadian biology with ferroptosis and provides a mechanistic link between time-dependent physiological regulation and structural organ damage, highlighting a potentially promising strategy for future hypertension intervention.

papers.title: Night Shift Work and Self-Reported Health Problems Among Hospital Workers in Mogadishu, Somalia: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Night shift work disrupts circadian rhythms and sleep and has been linked to physical, psychological and occupational health problems. Evidence from Somalia, where hospitals operate with severe staff shortages and limited occupational health support, is scarce. To describe night shift work characteristics and the prevalence of self-reported physical, psychological and occupational health problems among hospital workers who work night shifts in Mogadishu, Somalia. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted between January and June 2026 among 300 hospital workers recruited by purposive sampling from randomly selected public and private hospitals in Mogadishu. Nurses, doctors, laboratory staff, midwives, pharmacists and other hospital staff who had worked night shifts for at least six months completed a structured, self-administered questionnaire developed by the research team, in which each health problem was recorded as a single yes/no item. Prevalence is reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Most participants worked rotating shifts (60.7%), 68.7% worked night shifts of 12 hours or longer, and 68.0% were dissatisfied with their shift schedule. The most frequently reported problems were stress (78.7%; 95% CI 73.7-82.9), frequent fatigue (76.0%; 70.9-80.5), sleep problems (71.3%; 66.0-76.2), reduced concentration (68.7%; 63.2-73.7), headaches (64.0%; 58.4-69.2), anxiety (62.7%; 57.1-67.9) and burnout symptoms (58.0%; 52.3-63.4), followed by gastrointestinal problems (39.3%; 34.0-45.0), hypertension symptoms (34.0%; 28.9-39.5) and work-related errors during night shifts (30.7%; 25.7-36.1). Self-reported sleep-related, physical, psychological and occupational problems were highly prevalent among night shift hospital workers in Mogadishu. Because the study was descriptive and cross-sectional, with no day-shift comparison group, the findings show the burden of these problems but do not establish that night shift work caused them. Hospital leaders should review shift scheduling and strengthen occupational and mental health support, and longitudinal studies using validated instruments are needed.

papers.title: Case Report: Electroencephalography-informed low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting the supplementary motor area in severe functional movement disorder.
papers.abstract: Functional movement disorder (FMD) is increasingly being recognized as a condition associated with abnormal brain network connectivity; however, effective treatment strategies remain limited. We report the case of a patient with severe FMD that developed following an occupational injury and was characterized by functional tremors accompanied by migraines and prominent autonomic symptoms. Based on electroencephalography (EEG) network analysis, low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting the supplementary motor area was administered, followed by staged rehabilitation incorporating visual feedback. The combined intervention reduced tremors and improved gait speed, activities of daily living, and EEG network connectivity. This case highlights the potential utility of combining EEG-guided neuromodulation with staged rehabilitation for the treatment of FMD and supports further investigation of this approach.

papers.title: Real-time monitoring of root dielectric properties for assessing crop plant damage caused by foliar application of glyphosate.
papers.abstract: There is a knowledge gap regarding how foliar injury and restricted water uptake can be detected by measuring root dielectric response. This pot study nondestructively evaluated the efficiency of real-time dielectric measurement to monitor the effects of glyphosate spraying. Root dielectric properties were recorded on a minute scale in control and glyphosate-treated maize, cucumber, and pea. Chlorophyll, stomatal conductance, and biomass measurements were taken to interpret the dielectric changes. Electrical capacitance and conductance varied diurnally due to the circadian regulation of water uptake and hydraulic conductance. Glyphosate application reduced capacitance, indicating the impeded root growth and activity caused by impaired amino acid synthesis, foliar damage, and restricted transpiration. The dissipation factor decreased in response to glyphosate due to impeded apoplastic water flow, suppressed root lignification, and hampered water absorption. The enhanced leaf and root hydraulic resistance caused by glyphosate was manifested in sharply reduced electrical conductance. Changes in the species' dielectric response were consistent with physiological symptoms and biomass loss. Real-time dielectric measurement proved suitable for the nondestructive monitoring of plant responses to foliar stress through altered root traits. This method could be employed to evaluate herbicide tolerance in crops and to develop and determine dosage of herbicide ingredients.

papers.title: A technical review of dynamic brain functional imaging combined with EEG spectral parameters in the screening of early-stage brain injury.
papers.abstract: Early-stage brain injury encompasses subtypes such as mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), silent stroke and subclinical brain injury. It is characterised by negative imaging findings, subtle symptoms and a high risk of long-term neurological deficits, presenting a key challenge in the early screening and prevention of neurological diseases. Traditional imaging techniques, such as structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT), can only identify organic morphological lesions. Their detection rate for early micro-injuries at the level of neuronal electrophysiology and brain network function is extremely low. Consequently, these techniques struggle to meet the clinical needs for early screening, assessment, and intervention. Electroencephalography (EEG) spectral changes (including conventional spectral slowing and 1/f aperiodic abnormalities) and large-scale dynamic neural network disruption across the entire brain are core pathological features of early brain functional damage; they may serve as indirect correlates of microscopic pathological changes such as an imbalance in neuronal excitation-inhibition and abnormalities in the efficiency of brain information transmission. Based on this, this paper proposes a Dynamic-Spectral Coupling (DSC) framework, which proposes spectral abnormalities as a potential upstream mechanism associated with network reorganisation. Within this framework, this narrative review summarizes dynamic functional magnetic resonance imaging (dynamic fMRI), EEG spectral analysis and multimodal fusion technologies, with a particular focus on elucidating the coupling mechanisms between EEG periodic and 1/f aperiodic spectral parameters and dynamic brain network indicators. The review outlines the screening value and application advantages of multimodal fusion technologies in mTBI, occult cerebrovascular injury and subclinical brain injury. Furthermore, the paper summarises the current limitations of these technologies in terms of clinical translation, methodology and database development. Taking into account the clinical needs of neurorehabilitation, it proposes future development directions, including the development of lightweight devices, AI-assisted diagnosis, the establishment of standardised analytical systems and the translation of precision rehabilitation. The aim is to provide technical guidance and theoretical support for screening, risk stratification and rehabilitation planning in early-stage brain injury, while acknowledging that clinical utility remains to be established.

papers.title: Plasma Biomarkers Differentiate Cognitive Impairment in Postmenopausal Women with Insomnia Disorder.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep disorders are common in postmenopausal women and may contribute to cognitive decline. We investigated whether plasma biomarkers differentiate cognitive impairment (CI) in this population. Methods: In this cross-sectional exploratory study, we recruited 105 outpatients with insomnia disorder (79 women and 26 men) aged 45-60 years with insomnia symptoms (PSQI > 5, ISI > 7). Cognition was assessed using the Chinese Brief Cognitive Test (CBCT) and Auditory Verbal Learning Test. Postmenopausal women were classified as CI or non-CI based on CBCT criteria. Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain, orexin A, total tau, and phosphorylated tau-181 (p-Tau) were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Associations with cognition and exploratory classification performance were examined using correlation and receiver operating characteristic analyses. Results: Postmenopausal women exhibited higher anxiety and poorer cognitive performance despite comparable insomnia severity. Among them (non-CI n=42; CI n=37), the CI group had higher plasma GFAP (14.82 vs. 12.42 ng/mL, P = .004) and p-Tau (1,002.18 vs. 918.27 pg/mL, P = .034). Biomarker-cognition correlations were weak. GFAP showed the highest apparent performance among individual biomarkers (area under the curve, AUC = 0.672). The clinical information-adjusted model incorporating orexin A, GFAP, and p-Tau showed the highest apparent AUC among biomarker combinations (AUC = 0.755), although internally validated performance was more modest. Conclusions: Plasma GFAP and p-Tau, with potential incremental contribution from orexin A, may provide exploratory information for identifying cognitive vulnerability in postmenopausal women with insomnia disorder. These exploratory findings require validation in larger and independent cohorts.

papers.title: Effect of Internet-Based Psychological Treatments on Anxiety and Depression in Breast Cancer Patients.
papers.abstract: To assess the effectiveness and long-term impact of internet-based psychological interventions on anxiety, depression, and quality of life in breast cancer (BC) patients. Data were collected from 150 BC patients treated at the Third Hospital of Nanchang. Patients were assigned to either the research group (n=71), receiving internet-based therapies, or the control group (n=79), undergoing traditional psychological interventions. Psychological parameters were assessed using validated scales, including the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC), Piper Fatigue Scale (PFS), Fear of Disease Progression Questionnaire - Short Form (FoP-Q-SF), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the Cancer Treatment Quality of Life Core Questionnaire (EORTC-QLQ-C30). The research group showed significantly lower Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale - Anxiety (HADS-A), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale - Depression (HADS-D), and FoP-Q-SF scores than the control group at 1 month post intervention (T1) (P < .05). At 3 months (T2) and 6 months (T3) post-intervention, the research group had higher CD-RISC scores and lower HADS-A, HADS-D, and FoP-Q-SF scores compared to the control group (P < .05). Within-group comparisons revealed that PFS scores increased at T1, while FoP-Q-SF scores decreased and EORTC-QLQ-C30 scores improved significantly at T2 (P < .05). By T3, PFS and FoP-Q-SF scores were significantly reduced compared to T0 (P < .05). Internet-based psychological treatments demonstrated superior efficacy in reducing anxiety and depression among BC patients compared to conventional interventions, with sustained effects observed over 6 months. These findings underscore the potential of online psychological therapies as a viable intervention for improving mental health outcomes in BC patients.

papers.title: Impact of nocturnal oxygen saturation on sleep quality and exercise performance in adult Fontan patients.
papers.abstract: A decreased peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) is common in Fontan patients. We aimed to determine whether these patients experience greater nocturnal desaturation (ΔSpO2,noct), and to which extent this may impact sleep quality and exercise performance, compared to healthy controls. 16 adult Fontan patients and 16 healthy, individually matched controls completed questionnaires on quality of life, sleep quality, and daytime sleepiness, performed measurements of lung function and diffusion capacity (DLCO), and cycled in a cardiopulmonary exercise test to volitional exhaustion. Sleep quality was assessed with a wrist-worn actigraph and nocturnal SpO2 was measured with a pulse oximeter during six nights. Fontan patients experienced greater ΔSpO2,noct (-3.4 ± 0.8%-points, n = 14) compared to their controls (-2.5 ± 0.6%-points, n = 14, p = 0.001). In patients, ΔSpO2,noct correlated with baseline SpO2, DLCO, and exercise performance. Fontan patients had a longer sleep onset latency (22.8 ± 9.6 vs. 10.8 ± 6.0 min, p < 0.001) and lower self-perceived physical functioning (91 ± 7 vs. 100 ± 0 points, p < 0.001), but similar subjective sleep quality (4.2 ± 1.5 vs. 3.4 ± 1.4 points, p = 0.121) and daytime sleepiness (6.1 ± 4.3 vs. 6.3 ± 2.8 points, p = 0.884) compared to controls. In patients, daytime sleepiness correlated with the total number of desaturation events (r = 0.74, p = 0.003). Indices of nocturnal SpO2 were related to daytime sleepiness and reduced exercise performance, and may therefore be a contributing factor to exercise limitation in adult Fontan patients. Enhancing nocturnal SpO2 may thus be a promising target to improve daytime sleepiness and exercise performance in adult Fontan patients.
authors: Kyle G P J M Boyle
papers.journal: International journal of cardiology. Congenital heart disease

papers.title: Neurodynamical heterogeneous spiking neural network for spatiotemporal cognitive signal processing.
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) enable low-power brain-inspired computing via sparse binary spike transmission. Nevertheless, conventional homogeneous SNNs built exclusively upon leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons exhibit limited capacity for complex multi-scale temporal cognitive dynamics. Existing parametric-heterogeneous SNNs only tune internal hyperparameters within single-compartment LIF units and cannot capture diverse neuronal computations observed in biological circuits. Drawing inspiration from cross-neuronal dynamical heterogeneity in neural systems for multi-dimensional perception and cognition, this work proposes the Neurodynamical Heterogeneous Spiking Neural Network (NHSNN). NHSNN integrates three functionally distinct spiking neuron models: LIF, dendrite-inspired Pinsky-Rinzel (PR), and leaky resonate-and-fire (LRF), with each neuron type strategically assigned to dedicated functional modules to realise cross-neuronal heterogeneous spike encoding. We evaluate NHSNN across three representative cognitive-signal modalities: clinical electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, rhythmic auditory music data, and textual semantic sequences. On EEG-diagnosis and music-classification benchmarks, NHSNN achieves accuracy on a comparable scale relative to mainstream full-precision artificial neural networks (ANNs), though cross-study comparisons require caution owing to differing experimental protocols; on textual semantic tasks, it obtains accuracy comparable to existing SNN alternatives. Under matched network dimensionality, our approach substantially reduces parameter overhead while preserving intrinsic spike-driven energy advantages. Ablation and controlled baseline experiments verify that complementary cross-neuronal dynamical synergy - rather than raw increase of model complexity - yields strong multi-modal representations and removes requirements for heavy auxiliary modules. By balancing biological inspiration, temporal modeling capacity and computational efficiency, NHSNN provides a lightweight neuromorphic paradigm for resource-constrained edge cognitive-computing scenarios.
