papers.title: Effect of Melatonin on 24-Hour Urinary Protein Excretion and Sleep Quality in Patients With Stage 3-4 Chronic Kidney Disease: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract: Proteinuria is an established marker of renal injury and is closely associated with adverse outcomes in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Melatonin has attracted interest as a potential renoprotective agent because of its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and regulatory effects on several pathways implicated in kidney injury. However, clinical data regarding its effects on proteinuria in patients with non-dialysis CKD are limited. This trial investigated whether melatonin supplementation alters 24-h urinary protein excretion in adults with stage 3-4 CKD. We conducted a 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial in adults with stage 3-4 CKD and persistent proteinuria. Seventy-three participants were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive either oral melatonin (3 mg at bedtime) or a matching placebo. The prespecified primary endpoint was the change in 24-h urinary protein excretion between baseline and week 12. Secondary assessments included renal function, blood pressure, sleep quality, metabolic and laboratory parameters, and treatment safety. A reduction in 24-h urinary protein excretion was observed in both treatment groups. The mean reduction was 52.45 ± 128.19 mg/day with melatonin and 28.69 ± 82.59 mg/day with placebo, yielding a between-group difference of -23.76 mg/day (95% CI, -74.08 to 26.56; p = 0.92). Serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate remained largely stable during follow-up. Compared with placebo, melatonin was associated with a significant reduction in total cholesterol. Sleep quality also showed a statistically significant difference in the change in PSQI score between groups, with mean changes of -0.18 ± 0.84 and -0.69 ± 1.06 in the melatonin and placebo groups, respectively (p = 0.047). No treatment-related serious adverse events were observed. In adults with stage 3-4 CKD, 12 weeks of melatonin supplementation at 3 mg nightly did not demonstrate a clinically meaningful reduction in 24-h urinary protein excretion compared with placebo. Although the point estimate favored melatonin, the confidence interval was compatible with both a modest benefit and no treatment effect. Melatonin was generally well tolerated and was associated with modest changes in selected metabolic and sleep-related outcomes. Larger, multicenter trials with longer follow-up and adequate statistical power are needed to determine whether melatonin has clinically relevant renal effects in specific CKD populations. Trial Registration: This clinical trial was registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT No. IRCT20160412027346N12).

papers.title: Insomnia and medication overuse headache: neurobiological links, reciprocal interactions, and integrated therapeutic strategies.
papers.abstract: Medication overuse headache (MOH) and insomnia are not merely coincidental companions: each measurably worsens the severity and treatment response of the other. Whether this association reflects a genuine reciprocal influence, a shared constitutional vulnerability, or some combination of both carries direct practical consequences for clinical decision-making. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from Mendelian randomization genetics, polysomnographic cohort studies, pharmacological withdrawal trials, and mechanistic neurobiology, based on a search of PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar through 20 June 2026. Genetic analyses are compatible with a directional association between insomnia liability and migraine risk, although causation is not established and the instruments capture migraine broadly rather than the MOH phenotype, a limitation that applies to all causal inferences in this review. In the other direction, opioids, barbiturates, and triptans each disrupt sleep architecture through mechanisms specific to their molecular targets, and questionnaire-based withdrawal studies consistently report parallel improvements in sleep quality and headache frequency. Three neurobiological substrates appear centrally involved: orexinergic dysregulation, melatonin suppression, and glial neuroinflammation. Together, they may sustain a self-reinforcing cycle that neither detoxification alone nor sleep treatment alone can fully dismantle. The COMISA phenotype (comorbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea) and concurrent psychiatric illness compound treatment resistance and raise relapse rates at one year. Objective polysomnographic evidence that sleep architecture actually recovers after drug withdrawal is absent from the literature - a gap that limits the mechanistic conclusions that can be drawn. The available evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that concurrent medication withdrawal, CBT-I, preventive pharmacotherapy - including anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies - and CPAP where indicated may yield better outcomes than sequential management, but this hypothesis has not been tested in a randomized controlled trial. Designing that trial is the most pressing research need in this field.

papers.title: Asthma burden and its impact on health-related quality of life among school adolescents in Anuradhapura district, Sri Lanka.
papers.abstract: Asthma is a common chronic airway disease in adolescents, causing respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough. Asthma significantly impacts health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Its prevalence and symptom patterns in Southeast Asia, particularly among Sri Lankan adolescents, are not well known. To assess the prevalence of asthma and its impact on the quality of life in Sri Lankan adolescents. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1099 adolescents aged 13-15 years in mixed-gender schools in the Anuradhapura district, Sri Lanka (46.4% boys, mean age 14.03 years). The International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Childhood questionnaire was used to assess asthma prevalence. Students with physician-diagnosed asthma and wheezing in the previous 12 months were categorized as having current asthma. The PedsQL inventory was used to assess HRQoL. The prevalence of current asthma, physician-diagnosed asthma, and severe asthma was 13.8% [95% confidence interval (CI): 11.8-15.8], 20.2% (95%CI: 17.8-22.5), and 4.6% (95%CI: 3.4-5.8), respectively. Exercise-induced wheeze, sleep, and speech disturbances were significantly associated with asthma (P < 0.001). Overall, HRQoL was consistently reduced across all asthma diagnostic categories (current asthma, physician-diagnosed asthma, and severe asthma) compared with adolescents without asthma (P < 0.001). There is a significant burden of asthma among adolescents, with 13.8% having current asthma and 4.6% having severe asthma. Adolescents with current asthma have reduced HRQoL compared to non-asthmatics, highlighting the need for comprehensive management strategies beyond symptom control.

papers.title: Chronic circadian misalignment in military personnel: a potential contributor to neuroinflammation risk.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythm disruption is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to neurological disorders; however, its role is often viewed as a secondary consequence rather than a primary driver of brain dysfunction. We argue that chronic circadian misalignment should be reconceptualized as a potential, modifiable contributor to neuroinflammatory risk, rather than viewed solely as a secondary consequence. Military personnel represent a unique and underutilized human model in this context, as they are chronically exposed to predictable circadian stressors, including irregular training schedules, overseas travel, sleep restriction, and pre-operational stress. At the molecular level, circadian misalignment disrupts core clock gene regulation (e.g., CLOCK, BMAL1), leading to downstream alterations in mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis. These changes promote a sustained pro-inflammatory milieu, impair neuroimmune balance, and compromise synaptic plasticity and blood-brain barrier integrity. We propose that these mechanisms collectively increase vulnerability to cognitive dysfunction and mood disturbances, even in otherwise healthy and physically fit populations. Thus, circadian misalignment in military personnel is not merely a byproduct of performance demands, but a biologically plausible contributor to brain dysfunction that warrants targeted intervention and further mechanistic study. Reframing circadian disruption as a potential, modifiable neurobiological risk factor has significant implications for both research and practice.

papers.title: Investigating the Association between Sleep Problems and Physical Activity in Children with Cerebral Palsy: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Given the significance of sleep and physical activity (PA) as modifiable factors influencing overall health and development in childhood, this study aims to examine the association between sleep problems and PA levels in children with cerebral palsy (CP) and to compare these findings with typically developing (TD) children. This cross-sectional observational study included 40 children aged 6-12 years. The participant group comprised 20 children diagnosed with CP, exhibiting Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) levels I-II, and 20 age- and sex-matched TD peers. PA was measured using MOX accelerometers worn continuously for 24 hours on weekdays. Sleep habits were assessed using the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), both completed by parents. Children with CP demonstrated significantly lower levels of light, moderate, and vigorous PA compared to children with TD (p < 0.05). No significant difference was observed in total sleep habit scores between the groups (p = 0.423). A significant positive correlation was found between moderate PA and sleep habit in the CP group (r = 0.49, p = 0.03). Among children with TD, those with sleep problems engaged in significantly less vigorous PA than those without (p = 0.044). Children with CP exhibit lower PA levels than their TD peers. In this population, moderate-intensity PA appears to have a positive effect on sleep problems. Promoting moderate PA may contribute to improved sleep and overall health in children with CP. These findings highlight the importance of integrated PA and sleep health strategies in pediatric rehabilitation.

papers.title: Associations of self-reported physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep duration with mental and behavioral health among civil aviation flight students: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To examine the associations of self-reported physical activity at different intensities, total sedentary time, and sleep duration with mental and behavioral health indicators among civil aviation flight students. A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted at a civil aviation university from January 5 to 30, 2026. A total of 776 students majoring in Flight Technology were included, of whom 774 (99.7%) were male. Because only two participants were female, the primary inferential analyses were restricted to male participants. Physical activity and sedentary behavior were assessed using modified self-report items. Physical activity duration represented participants' self-reported activity time on a typical activity day rather than average daily or weekly physical activity time; sleep exposure was assessed using categorical self-reported sleep duration. Depression, anxiety, stress, and problematic Internet use were assessed using validated scales. Generalized estimating equation models were used to examine cross-sectional associations between the behavioral indicators and outcomes, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction. In the fully adjusted male sample, after FDR correction, longer self-reported vigorous-intensity physical activity duration on a typical activity day was associated with lower anxiety scores; self-reported sleep duration <7 h was associated with higher depression, anxiety, stress, and problematic Internet use scores; and longer self-reported total sedentary time was associated with higher problematic Internet use scores. No statistically significant linear associations were observed between moderate- or light-intensity physical activity and any outcome after FDR correction. The observed associations were generally small: the association between vigorous-intensity physical activity and anxiety was approximately 0.10 outcome standard deviations, the associations between sleep duration <7 h and the corresponding outcomes were approximately 0.24-0.27 standard deviations, and the association between total sedentary time and problematic Internet use was approximately 0.04 standard deviations. The directions of the main associations were generally consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses, although the strength of statistical evidence for some associations varied by outcome definition, sample restriction, and data-processing approach. Among male civil aviation flight students, self-reported physical activity, total sedentary time, and sleep duration were cross-sectionally associated with selected mental and behavioral health indicators. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings cannot establish causality, an optimal physical activity dose, a sleep intervention threshold, or time-substitution effects between behaviors. The findings suggest that behavioral indicators and mental and behavioral health status may be considered jointly in this population, but the observed associations require confirmation in longitudinal studies using objective, device-based behavioral measures.

papers.title: Assessing selective outcome reporting in sleep disorder trials: A registry-publication comparison study.
papers.abstract: Prespecified outcomes form the foundation of clinical trial validity. Despite federal registration requirements under the FDAAA Final Rule, discrepancies between registered and published outcomes remain common across medical fields. The extent of outcome modifications in interventional sleep disorder trials has not been systematically examined using registry version histories. We conducted a cross-sectional registry-publication comparison of 54 interventional sleep disorder trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov between January 2017 and December 2024. Using the platform's "History of Changes" tool, we compared earliest and most recent registry versions to identify outcome modifications. Changes were classified as high, moderate, or low impact. Corresponding publications were reviewed to assess disclosure. Predictors of modification were evaluated using Firth penalized logistic regression. Substantive outcome modifications were present in 94.4% of trials, with a median of five modifications per trial. High-impact modifications affecting primary outcomes occurred in 48.1% of trials. Changes most frequently involved clarification or increased specification (61.1%), outcome additions (57.4%), and removals (40.7%). The majority of modifications occurred after primary completion (60.8%) or publication (37.3%). Disclosure was rare: 3.9% of trials acknowledged modifications in the registry and 5.9% in the corresponding publication. Industry funding was associated with lower odds of high-impact modification (OR 0.2, 95% CI 0.0-0.7; p = 0.01). Outcome modifications are nearly universal in sleep disorder trials and are rarely disclosed. Strengthening preregistration practices, editorial oversight, and registry transparency may improve the reliability of the sleep medicine evidence base.

papers.title: Low-intensity mind-body exercise for mental health in ageing societies: Tai Chi as a scalable intervention across depression, anxiety, insomnia, loneliness, and cognitive decline.
papers.abstract: Population ageing is increasing the number of older adults who experience overlapping depressive symptoms, anxiety, insomnia, loneliness, and cognitive vulnerability, often alongside multimorbidity, pain, frailty, and functional limitation. This structured narrative review evaluates Tai Chi as a scalable, low-intensity mind-body exercise for these interconnected problems. We synthesised 171 publications identified through PubMed and citation chaining, including Tai Chi-specific clinical studies, broader mind-body evidence, guidelines, and implementation literature. Evidence is most consistent for reducing depressive symptoms, improving sleep, and improving balance, with possible benefits for selected cognitive outcomes. Evidence is weaker for diagnosed depressive or anxiety disorders, loneliness as a primary outcome, long-term cognitive trajectories, and dementia incidence. Tai Chi should therefore be positioned as an adjunct to established care, not as a replacement for pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), or multidomain dementia-risk reduction. Proposed pathways include autonomic regulation, sleep stabilisation, behavioral activation, balance confidence, cognitive-motor integration, and group participation; however, most mechanism evidence is indirect or exploratory. Translation requires clearly specified protocols, active comparators, blinded outcome assessments where feasible, long-term follow-up, systematic adverse-event reporting, cost-effectiveness analyses, and equity-focused implementation. Tai Chi is the most credible as an adaptable component of stepped or integrated care for older adults, provided that programmes are standardised, safely delivered, and evaluated against clinically significant outcomes.

papers.title: An automated EEG-ECG framework for CAP-HRV analysis: enabling brain-heart coupling studies in sleep disorders.
papers.abstract: Multimodal sleep analysis typically requires separate processing pipelines for electroencephalography (EEG) and electrocardiography (ECG), which complicates joint investigation of sleep microstructure and autonomic regulation. Cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) scoring and heart rate variability (HRV) analysis are routinely performed in different software environments, limiting temporal alignment, reproducibility, and scalability. We present an open-source MATLAB framework that integrates rule-based CAP A1 detection and HRV feature extraction within a single, time-synchronized workflow. The pipeline performs standardized EEG and ECG preprocessing, rule-based CAP A1 detection during slow-wave sleep (SWS) implementing the Terzano scoring criteria, R-peak detection via the Pan-Tompkins algorithm, and computation of time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear HRV features by calling the open-source PhysioZoo/mhrv toolbox directly. CAP annotations are aligned with 5-minute ECG epochs through the shared polysomnography (PSG) time base. The complete code is released as an open-source repository to support reuse and extension. Because HRV features are computed by calling the PhysioZoo/mhrv toolbox directly, the pipeline introduces no reimplemented HRV routine and inherits that toolbox's validated feature definitions. CAP A1 detection is provided as a rule-based implementation of published criteria and has not yet been benchmarked against expert manual scoring. A worked example on the OSAD+ subgroup (n = 18) demonstrates pipeline output across CAP and non-CAP epochs, and a healthy-sleep A1-event HRV reference is reported from the public CAP Sleep Database (15 controls, 785 A1 epochs) as a descriptive cross-database reference. The framework provides a reproducible, rule-based, and modular tool for integrated EEG-ECG analysis of sleep microstructure and autonomic dynamics. By enabling synchronized CAP-HRV feature extraction in a single environment, it lowers the engineering barrier to brain-heart coupling research during sleep and provides a foundation for future extensions, including validated CAP detection, a matched-control study, a Python port, and cloud-based deployment.

papers.title: Psychological support for depression and anxiety across chronic illness contexts: a comparative evaluation of three general-purpose AI chatbots.
papers.abstract: Digital mental health tools, including general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, may provide accessible and low-threshold psychological support for people living with chronic conditions. However, their value in this population depends not only on recognizing depression or anxiety, but also on understanding how psychological distress is shaped by disease-specific experiences and when self-guided support should transition toward professional care. We evaluated the appropriateness, contextual sensitivity, safety, and consistency of psychological support provided by three widely accessible AI chatbots across contrasting chronic illness contexts. We conducted a standardized simulated-patient benchmarking study comparing ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao. Twenty scenarios were developed across type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), representing matched mild and moderate presentations of depression and anxiety together with condition-specific distress related to diabetes self-management and CSU-related flare uncertainty. Each scenario was independently submitted to all three systems in two testing rounds, yielding 120 responses. Blinded raters assessed overall psychological support appropriateness, recognition and emotional support, chronic-illness contextualization, psychological support and referral, psychosomatic balance and safety, and major clinical or safety errors. Repeated testing assessed response consistency. Overall psychological support appropriateness differed across systems (P = 0.002), with 90.0% of ChatGPT, 75.0% of Gemini, and 55.0% of Doubao responses meeting the prespecified appropriateness threshold. Recognition and emotional support was consistently strong across systems, whereas greater differences emerged in chronic-illness contextualization (P = 0.001), psychological support and referral (P = 0.002), and psychosomatic balance and safety (P<0.001). All responses to mild presentations were classified as psychologically appropriate, compared with 58.3% of responses to moderate presentations, indicating that performance became less reliable when digital support required stronger escalation toward professional assessment. Contextualization was also less consistent in CSU, particularly when responses needed to incorporate flare unpredictability, pruritus, sleep disruption, and illness uncertainty. Major clinical or safety errors occurred in 0%, 10.0%, and 15.0% of first-round ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao responses, respectively. Test-retest consistency was moderate and varied between systems. General-purpose AI chatbots show potential as accessible, self-guided digital mental health resources for people living with chronic conditions, particularly for recognizing distress and providing initial supportive guidance. Their current limitations emerge when effective support requires disease-specific contextualization, balanced interpretation of psychological and somatic factors, or escalation as symptoms become more severe. These findings identify important boundaries for the use of conversational AI in chronic-illness mental health care and suggest that implementation should emphasize context-sensitive guidance, severity-responsive referral, and clear integration with rather than substitution for professional care.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification in Machine Learning for Biosignal Applications - A Review.
papers.abstract: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) has gained traction in an attempt to improve the interpretability and robustness of machine learning predictions. Specifically (medical) biosignals such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrocardiography (ECG), electrooculography (EOG), and electromyography (EMG) could benefit from good UQ, since these suffer from a poor signal-to-noise ratio, and good human interpretability is pivotal for medical applications. To determine how uncertainty estimation can be used for biosignal tasks, we investigate current methods, use cases, applications, evaluations, and uncertainty measures. In this paper, we systematically review the state of the art of applying Uncertainty Quantification to Machine Learning tasks in the biosignal domain. All works from Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE XPlore and PsycINFO that discuss uncertainty in Machine Learning on one of the aforementioned biosignals is included. We present various methods, shortcomings, uncertainty measures and theoretical frameworks that currently exist in this application domain based on the 53 reviewed papers and related literature. We address misconceptions in the field, provide recommendations for future work, and discuss gaps in the literature in relation to diagnostic implementations as well as control for prostheses or brain-computer interfaces. Overall it can be concluded that promising UQ methods are available, but that research is needed on how people and systems may interact with an uncertainty-model in a (clinical) environment.

papers.title: Venlafaxine in oncology: supportive-care evidence and emerging preclinical anticancer signals: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Venlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, has been investigated in oncology for several supportive care indications and, more recently, for potential anticancer activity. However, the available evidence remains fragmented across clinical and preclinical studies. This systematic review aimed to synthesize the available evidence regarding the role of venlafaxine in oncology, including established supportive care applications and emerging anticancer potential. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from database inception to 22 August 2026. Original clinical and preclinical studies evaluating venlafaxine in cancer populations or experimental cancer models were eligible. Clinical and preclinical evidence was synthesized separately using a narrative approach. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools for clinical studies and the SYRCLE Risk of Bias tool for animal studies. 25 studies were included, comprising 23 clinical studies and 2 preclinical studies. The strongest clinical evidence supported venlafaxine for treatment-related hot flashes, particularly among breast cancer survivors receiving endocrine therapy, with the strongest randomized, placebo-controlled trial evidence showing significantly greater reductions with venlafaxine than placebo (P < 0.0001 for higher doses); within-group percentage reductions are also reported but should not be interpreted as treatment effects. Evidence for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy was inconsistent, with potential benefit for acute oxaliplatin-related neurotoxicity but insufficient support for prevention or routine treatment of chronic CIPN. Evidence for other supportive care outcomes, including oral mucositis-associated pain, fatigue, sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and quality of life, was limited. Venlafaxine was generally well tolerated, although adverse effects varied by dose and comparator. Preclinical studies investigated anticancer activity, but not equivalently: one in melanoma models showed direct antiproliferative/pro-apoptotic effects of venlafaxine via JNK1/2-Nur77 signaling, whereas a colorectal cancer study showed only context-dependent antagonism of norepinephrine-driven tumor progression, with no significant effect of venlafaxine alone. No clinical evidence currently supports venlafaxine as a direct anticancer treatment. Venlafaxine has an established evidence-based role in supportive oncology for treatment-related hot flashes, whereas its role in CIPN and other supportive care indications remains uncertain. Emerging anticancer findings are limited to preclinical models and should be considered hypothesis-generating. Further randomized clinical trials are needed for supportive care indications, while additional mechanistic and preclinical validation is required before venlafaxine can be considered for clinical evaluation as an anticancer therapy.

papers.title: Sleep and Cognitive Performance: Exploring Benzodiazepine Receptor Agonist Use, Insomnia Symptoms, and Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: We hypothesized that benzodiazepine/z-drug (BZRA) dose, insomnia symptoms, and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) risk are associated with cognitive performance above and beyond other modifiable dementia risk factors. In this cross-sectional study, we used baseline data from recruited patients without dementia from one VA site and one academic site to analyze regression models based on previously published risk factors for cognitive impairment, adapted to include sleep and benzodiazepine usage interactions. Changes in R2 and model fit (F-tests) were examined for four nested regression models predicting Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Trail Making Test (TMT)-A, TMT-B, and Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST). Base Models included common dementia risk factors. Model-2 = Base + Insomnia Severity Index; Model-3 = Model-2 + dose; Model-4 = Model-3 + OSA risk; and Model-5 = Model-4 + OSA-BZRA. R2 for the base model predicting MMSE was 0.139 (n = 313), 0.241 for TMT-A (n = 298), 0.229 for TMT-B (n = 287), and 0.189 for DSST (n = 285). Model-5 R2 was 0.142 for MMSE, 0.246 for TMT-A, 0.238 for TMT-B, and 0.190 for DSST, with all F-test p-values >.145. Sleep disorder variables did not significantly explain additional variation in cognition performance. Studies with a wider range of cognitive performance are needed. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12126-026-09684-6.

papers.title: Traditional Chinese medicine-related interventions and the cGAS-STING axis in neuroinflammation: disease contexts and mechanisms of action.
papers.abstract: Research on traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-related interventions has shifted from overall phenotypic effects to defined neuroimmune targets. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) axis connects cytosolic DNA sensing with host defense and sterile inflammatory injury, but the functional direction of this pathway changes with disease context. This review organizes preclinical findings by pathological setting and site of action. It examines herbal formulas and natural compounds, followed by acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and related delivery systems. Several sterile injury models associate benefit with reduced pathway-related inflammation. Acute sleep deprivation provides an example of protection accompanying restored STING signaling. Early herpes simplex virus infection follows a different pattern: restoration of suppressed antiviral signaling improves host defense. In acute postoperative pain and cancer-induced bone pain models, increased STING-IFN-I signaling accompanies electroacupuncture-induced analgesia. Some interventions reduce mitochondrial DNA stimulation. Others act on cGAS or STING, with separate studies targeting STING trafficking. Downstream inflammatory and cell-death responses form the final level. Mechanistic attribution is strongest when genetic or pharmacological perturbation links pathway change to functional outcome; direct binding has been demonstrated for a small group of compounds. These findings support a context-sensitive framework for interpreting modulation direction that requires validation within individual disease models. Clinical translation will depend on reproducible formulation composition, effective brain exposure, and safety.

papers.title: The History of Child Neurology in Iran: From Ancient Times to the Present.
papers.abstract: To describe the historical development of child neurology in Iran, from early Persian-Islamic medical concepts of neurological disease to contemporary subspecialty practice, education, research, and service delivery. This narrative historical review synthesized accessible peer-reviewed publications, institutional histories, university and hospital documents, professional-society resources, and publicly available records concerning Persian medical scholarship, medical education, pediatric hospitals, subspecialty training, neonatal care, epilepsy services, newborn screening, and neurogenetics in Iran. When historical dates or attributions were inconsistent, they were interpreted cautiously and reported as approximate or unspecified. Early Persian and Islamic medical traditions, including the works associated with Rhazes, Avicenna, and Jorjani, documented observations relevant to seizures, paralysis, developmental disorders, and cranial nerve function, although child neurology was not yet a distinct specialty. Modern development was facilitated by nineteenth-century educational reform, especially Dar al-Funun, followed by the establishment of pediatric teaching and referral hospitals, including Bahrami Children's Hospital, Children's Medical Center, and Mofid Children's Hospital. Integration of medical education and health services after 1985 strengthened specialty training and referral systems. Contemporary child neurology includes structured two-year subspecialty training, pediatric clinical neurophysiology and epilepsy fellowship programs, long-term video-electroencephalography monitoring, epilepsy monitoring units, neonatal intensive care expansion, newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism and phenylketonuria, neurogenetic resources such as Iranome, dedicated research centers, and an indexed specialty journal. Persistent challenges include uneven regional access, economic constraints, sanctions-related procurement barriers, and workforce migration. Child neurology in Iran has evolved from descriptive neurological knowledge embedded in Persian-Islamic medicine into a hospital-based, research-oriented pediatric subspecialty. Future progress depends on retaining the specialist workforce, strengthening provincial referral pathways, expanding registries and genomic capacity, and improving resilience of clinical and research infrastructure.

papers.title: Validity evidence for the Clinic Screening Tool for HIV (CST-HIV) addressing factors that undermine health-related quality of life in people living with HIV.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the psychometric properties and clinical validity of the Clinic Screening Tool for HIV (CST-HIV) to determine whether the CST-HIV demonstrates a reliable multidimensional structure and clinically meaningful associations with established patient-reported outcome measures (PROM) and HIV clinical markers. A cross-sectional study was conducted within the Spanish CoRIS multicentre cohort, including 286 adults with HIV. Participants completed the CST-HIV and validated PROMs. Clinical indicators (CD4+ cell count and percentage, HIV-1 RNA viral load, and non-AIDS events) were collected at current and retrospective time points. Analyses included confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity, associations with clinical markers, and age-group comparisons. Confirmatory factor analysis showed good model fit, with satisfactory internal consistency across domains (ω = 0.86-0.89). CST-HIV shows convergent validity, including psychological distress with PHQ-4 (r = 0.79), anticipated stigma with HIV stigma (r = 0.65), sexuality with sexual satisfaction (r = -0.74), sleep and fatigue with insomnia severity (r = 0.79), and material deprivation with social exclusion (r = 0.67) (all p < 0.001). Anticipated stigma (ρ = -0.16, p = 0.014) and material deprivation (ρ = -0.18, p = 0.005) were associated with lower CD4+ counts, while material deprivation was associated with higher viral load (ρ = 0.13, p = 0.046). Sexual satisfaction was lower among participants aged ≥50 years (d = -0.47, p < 0.001). The CST-HIV demonstrates strong psychometric performance, supporting its use as a valid, brief, multidimensional screening tool to inform person-centered HIV care and clinical intervention.

papers.title: Association between social jetlag and diabetes self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes: a cross-sectional study with serial mediation analysis.
papers.abstract: Diabetes self-management requires consistent daily behaviors. Social jetlag, the mismatch between workday and free-day sleep timing, may disrupt daily behavior routines. This study examined the association between social jetlag and self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D), and whether sleep quality and depressive symptoms statistically accounted for portions of this association. This cross-sectional study recruited employed adults aged 18-60 years with T2D from the endocrinology departments of three tertiary public general hospitals in Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, China, from January to April 2026. Social jetlag was calculated from the micro Munich Chronotype Questionnaire; sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and diabetes self-management were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Patient Health Questionnaire-9, and Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities, respectively. Multivariable linear regression and serial mediation analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples were performed. A total of 339 participants were analyzed. Each additional h of social jetlag was associated with higher PSQI score (B = 1.352, 95% CI 1.042 to 1.663), higher PHQ-9 score (B = 3.772, 95% CI 3.314 to 4.229), and lower SDSCA score (B = -6.623, 95% CI -7.566 to -5.679). The direct association remained significant after PSQI and PHQ-9 scores were included (B = -3.830, 95% CI -5.048 to -2.611). The specific indirect association through depressive symptoms alone was -2.230 (95% bootstrap CI -3.053 to -1.469), and the serial indirect association through sleep quality and depressive symptoms was -0.314 (95% bootstrap CI -0.534 to -0.150). Greater social jetlag was associated with poorer diabetes self-management. Significant indirect associations were observed through depressive symptoms alone and through the serial pathway from sleep quality to depressive symptoms. These associations do not establish temporal ordering or causal mediation because the data were cross-sectional.

papers.title: A non-randomized trial of the effects of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation on cognitive performance and resting state connectivity.
papers.abstract: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) has shown promise for enhancing cognition and emotion regulation. To date, most human studies have focused on narrow learning paradigms that limit our understanding of how taVNS influences complex, integrative cognitive operations. Moreover, the underlying mechanisms of taVNS are still not well understood. Building on preclinical findings that vagus nerve stimulation enhances cognitive flexibility and memory in animal models, this study investigated whether acute taVNS can modulate executive function and neural connectivity in healthy adults. Using a quasi-experimental design, forty healthy participants received either active or sham taVNS while completing executive function tasks and adaptive cognitive training (BrainHQ). High-density electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded during stimulation to assess cortical activity and functional connectivity across frequency bands. Multivariate analyses demonstrated significant effects of taVNS on cognitive function and EEG. Post-hoc group comparisons showed that compared to sham stimulation, active taVNS was associated with improved BrainHQ performance and decreased delta-band connectivity in left frontal, central, and parietal regions. Delta-band connectivity during active taVNS was positively associated with pre-to-post improvements in mood. No difference in executive function tasks was found between active and sham taVNS. Sensitivity analyses using adjusted models showed that these effects were sensitive to age, sex, and education. By evaluating multiple dimensions of executive function, these exploratory findings suggest that active taVNS may influence selected aspects of executive performance and frontal-parietal delta connectivity, potentially reflecting enhanced neural efficiency arising from the interaction between vagally mediated neuromodulation and continuously adaptive cognitive demands. However, these effects did not survive multiple-comparison correction and should therefore be interpreted cautiously and replicated in larger, prospectively powered studies.

papers.title: Physical activity, metabolic health and well-being in community-dwelling older adults: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: Physical activity, sedentary time and sleep make up a closed 24-hour composition; reallocating time from one behavior to another has consequences for the metabolic profile and the well-being of the older adult. No single account has mapped which behaviors have been studied against which outcomes in this population. We conducted a scoping review to chart the exposures against the outcomes, summarize the associations, compare the assessment methods, and identify the gaps. Four databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus) were searched through May 2026, in line with the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR. Studies were eligible when they enrolled community-dwelling older adults with a mean age of 60 or above and reported a movement-behavior exposure against a metabolic or a well-being outcome. Database searches identified 21,995 records; 2,468 remained after de-duplication for title-and-abstract screening. Reference-list hand-searching yielded 193 additional citations, three of which proceeded to full-text assessment. Overall, 82 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility and 27 studies entered the charted evidence base. Cognition was the dominant well-being outcome; more activity and less sitting went with better cognitive performance across several cohorts. In one cross-sectional study of short-sleeping older adults, the cognitive benefit appeared to plateau at approximately 800-960 MET-minutes per week, although no other included study tested that threshold. The metabolic signal was real but thinner, and it rested largely on cross-sectional compositional work. Quality of life was rarely measured. The daily movement composition tracks with both the cardiometabolic and the well-being outcomes. Encouraging the older adult to move more, sit less and sleep adequately is supported by the direction of the evidence. What the field still lacks are the causal design, the quality-of-life outcome, and investigations that isolate activity from the surrounding lifestyle.

papers.title: In search of vitamin sleep: cross-sectional analysis of vitamin and mineral intake and sleep health outcomes in adolescents.
papers.abstract: Many U.S. youth fail to meet nutritional guidelines and often struggle with inadequate sleep. We examined how adolescent micronutrient intake is related to sleep. We hypothesized that higher intake of folic acid, potassium, calcium, magnesium, vitamin D, vitamin K, and iron would be associated with earlier chronotype, reduced daytime sleepiness, earlier DLMO timing, and less circadian misalignment. We also explored the relationship between sleep health outcomes and sodium, zinc, copper, selenium, vitamin C, niacin, vitamin B2, vitamin B6, folate, retinol, vitamin B1, vitamin B2, vitamin B12, vitamin A RAE, vitamin E, alpha carotene, beta carotene, lycopene, cryptoxanthin, and Lutein + zeaxanthin intake. Across two paradigms, 80 participants (ages 14-18) completed ASA-24 dietary recalls on 2-3 randomized days (weekday and weekend), dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) protocols, sleep health questionnaires, daily sleep diaries, and actigraphy. Using step-wise mixed effects models nested by subject, we explored connections between same-day micronutrient intake and same-night sleep, as well as average relationships across all recall days. No micronutrient emerged as significantly associated with improved sleep health across all models. Potassium (b's = -0.03 to 0.004, p's < 0.05) and retinol (b's = -0.20 to 0.01, p's < 0.05) showed the most consistent associations with positive sleep outcomes. Zinc (b's = -0.54 to 3.51, p's < 0.10), and vitamin B12 (b's = -0.96t to 7.22, p's < 0.05) were most consistently linked with negative sleep outcomes. These findings highlight potential relationships between micronutrient intake and adolescent sleep health. This can inform further research establishing causality and informing dietary-based sleep health interventions.

papers.title: Nocturnal sleep duration, clinical activity score, and thyroid functional remission after radioactive iodine therapy in Graves' disease with thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy.
papers.abstract: To examine whether pretreatment nocturnal sleep duration and Clinical Activity Score (CAS) are associated with thyroid functional remission after radioactive iodine (¹³¹I) therapy in Graves' disease (GD) with concomitant thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO). The primary endpoint was thyroid functional remission, not ocular cure. We retrospectively reviewed 153 patients at a single center (53 in remission; 100 not in remission), followed for at least 12 months after ¹³¹I therapy. Sleep duration and CAS were pretreatment baseline measures; 20 patients received prednisone before ¹³¹I therapy (discontinued ≥ 3 days prior) and 133 received none; no thyroid-directed or immunosuppressive treatment was given during follow-up. Remission was coded using the response categories of the 2021 Chinese Society of Nuclear Medicine ¹³¹I treatment guideline (euthyroidism or hypothyroidism vs. partial or ineffective response). Missing continuous values were multiply imputed (20 chains). Analyses included false discovery rate (FDR)-controlled univariate screening, cross-validated least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) selection, post-selection logistic regression, Firth sensitivity analysis, interaction tests, and mutually adjusted restricted cubic splines (RCS). No patient sleeping less than 6h achieved remission [0/31; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0%-9.2%]. After FDR adjustment, GD duration, TAO duration, sleep duration, and CAS remained associated with remission. LASSO (one-standard-error rule, C = 0.142) retained GD duration, sleep duration, and CAS. In the post-selection model, the odds ratio (OR) per month of GD duration was 0.991 (95% CI 0.979-1.003; P = 0.152); per additional sleep hour, 6.13 (95% CI 3.16-11.91; P < 0.001; Firth OR 5.64, 95% CI 2.99-10.63); and per CAS point, 0.64 (95% CI 0.48-0.86; P = 0.003). The CAS × sleep interaction was not significant (Wald P = 0.096; likelihood-ratio P = 0.086). Mutually adjusted RCS supported non-linearity for CAS (P < 0.001) but not for sleep (P = 0.585). Longer pretreatment nocturnal sleep and lower CAS were associated with thyroid functional remission after ¹³¹I therapy in this single-center cohort, with consistent directions across sensitivity models. These retrospective, post-selection associations require prospective validation; the absence of remission below 6h and the fitted threshold effects are exploratory post hoc observations, not validated thresholds.

papers.title: Case Report: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease initially misdiagnosed as ischemic stroke: a diagnostic challenge and biomarker-based clarification.
papers.abstract: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) is a rare and uniformly fatal prion disorder characterized by rapidly progressive dementia and heterogeneous neurological manifestations. Early sCJD may be misinterpreted as cerebrovascular disease, particularly when focal neurological deficits, unilateral diffusion abnormalities, and vascular risk factors coexist. We report a 76-year-old man with a history of hypertension who initially presented with dizziness and gait instability, followed by progressive right-sided weakness, and was initially diagnosed with ischemic stroke in the setting of intracranial arterial stenosis. Despite antiplatelet and vascular management, the patient experienced rapid cognitive decline, psychiatric disturbances, aphasia, and progressive hemiparesis. Follow-up MRI demonstrated progressive, non-territorial cortical ribbon-like diffusion restriction predominantly involving the left insular, parietal, frontal, and temporal cortices. CSF analysis revealed markedly elevated total tau (4553.50 pg/mL; laboratory-reported cutoff: < 399 pg/mL), phosphorylated tau (66.93 pg/mL; laboratory-reported cutoff: < 50 pg/mL), and 14-3-3γ protein (50515 AU/mL; laboratory-reported cutoff: < 20,000 AU/mL). Autoimmune encephalitis antibodies and metagenomic next-generation sequencing were negative. PRNP genetic testing detected no pathogenic variant in the patient and his son. EEG showed diffuse slowing without periodic sharp wave complexes. According to the 2017 International CJD Surveillance Network criteria, the diagnosis was classified as probable sCJD on the basis of rapidly progressive cognitive impairment, two clinical features (documented cerebellar ataxia and pyramidal signs), characteristic MRI abnormalities, and positive CSF 14-3-3; the typical EEG criterion was absent and RT-QuIC was not performed. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of early sCJD initially misdiagnosed as ischemic stroke in the presence of coexisting vascular pathology. Recognition of non-vascular diffusion patterns, careful reassessment of atypical clinical progression, and adjunctive CSF biomarker assessment may facilitate timely diagnostic reconsideration and help avoid unnecessary interventions.

papers.title: Prevalence and co-occurrence of behavioral risk factors for noncommunicable diseases among working-age adults attending primary care in Bosnia and Herzegovina: a multicenter cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To assess the prevalence and co-occurrence of established behavioral risk factors for noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) among the working-age population attending family medicine clinics across Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH). This cross-sectional study enrolled clinically stable individuals aged 18 to 65 years attending family medicine clinics across BiH. We assessed the prevalence and distribution of behavioral risk factors for NCDs using a standardized questionnaire and compared them by sex, socio-economic status, age groups, place of residence, and NCD status. The study included 2112 participants, of whom 584 (28%) had an NCD. The most prevalent behavioral risk factors were insufficient daily intake of fruit (85%), fiber (71%), and water (69%), followed by high salt consumption (66%) and physical inactivity (65%). The prevalence of overweight was 57% and it was significantly higher in men than in women. Men reported higher smoking rates but had higher levels of physical activity and greater water intake. Women demonstrated healthier dietary patterns and significantly higher fruit and fiber intake. Participants with NCDs had a better diet than those without NCDs, but reported worse stress management and sleep quality, which might reflect behavioral changes following disease onset. Behavioral risk factors for NCDs are widespread among the working-age population in BiH, with suboptimal diet, physical inactivity, and smoking being the most prevalent ones. Public health policies should be focused on disease prevention, such as health-promoting infrastructure and education for health care professionals and patients.

papers.title: Distress, emotional well-being, and sleep quality in daily life: A dual-continuum perspective.
papers.abstract: We examined whether daily distress and emotional well-being form related but distinguishable dimensions, as suggested by a dual-continuum perspective, and how they relate to perceived sleep quality. Evening diaries assessed these variables in 831 university students over 14 days. Emotional well-being comprised positive affect and life satisfaction, whereas distress comprised emotional exhaustion, depressed affect, anxiety, and negative affect. Multilevel confirmatory factor analysis supported two correlated within-person higher order factors over a single higher order factor, with a factor correlation of -.501. A Bayesian multilevel vector autoregressive model of order 1 (VAR(1)) estimated adjacent-day associations. Higher-than-usual distress predicted lower subsequent emotional well-being (β = -.032, 95% credible interval [CrI] [-.053, -.012]). Distress predicted poorer perceived quality of the subsequent sleep episode (β = -.057, 95% CrI [-.078, -.037]), and sleep quality reported at the preceding diary occasion predicted lower current distress (β = -.024, 95% CrI [-.043, -.004]) and higher emotional well-being (β = .021, 95% CrI [.001, .040]). The paths from emotional well-being to subsequent distress and sleep quality had 95% CrIs that included zero. The within-person measurement structure is consistent with a dual-continuum perspective on daily distress and emotional well-being.

papers.title: The Moderating Effect of Sleep Duration on the Association Between Chronic Disease and Health-Related Quality of Life in Middle-Aged Women.
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional secondary data analysis aimed to examine the association between the number of chronic diseases and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in middle-aged women and to determine whether sleep duration moderated this association. Data from 3062 women aged 46-70 years were obtained from the 2019 and 2021 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys. Complex-samples t-tests, analysis of variance, and multiple regression analyses were conducted. A significant moderating effect of sleep duration was observed for the > 9 h/day group compared with the > 6-7 h/day reference group (p = 0.016), with a stronger negative association between the number of chronic diseases and HRQOL in this group. Participants in the > 6-7 h/day and > 7-8 h/day groups reported significantly higher HRQOL than those sleeping ≤ 5, > 8-9, and > 9 h/day (p < 0.001), and a greater number of chronic diseases was associated with lower HRQOL (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that sleep duration, particularly sleep duration of more than 9 h, may be considered when evaluating the association between the number of chronic diseases and HRQOL among middle-aged women.

papers.title: Validation of the Telephone MoCA in iRBD and Parkinson's Disease with Conversion to the Standard MoCA.
papers.abstract: Telephone-based cognitive assessment may improve follow-up when face-to-face testing is impractical. The Telephone Montreal Cognitive Assessment (T-MoCA) omits visually dependent items from the standard MoCA, but its validity in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), remains uncertain. To assess agreement between the T-MoCA and face-to-face MoCA-22 in iRBD and PD, and derive and externally validate a MoCA-22 to MoCA-30 conversion. In the Oxford Parkinson's Disease Centre (OPDC) Discovery Cohort, 137 participants (38 controls, 47 iRBD, 52 PD) completed T-MoCA and MoCA-22 assessments. Agreement was evaluated using Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, Bland-Altman analysis, and equivalence testing with ±1-point bounds. Equipercentile equating with log-linear smoothing was used to derive a MoCA-22 to MoCA-30 conversion using Discovery data (3561 tests), with validation in Tracking Parkinson's (5767 tests) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (5047 tests). T-MoCA and face-to-face MoCA-22 scores were statistically equivalent, with minimal bias; 83.3% of scores differed by ≤1 point. However, concordance between test formats was moderate (Lin's CCC = 0.58). Across 14,375 MoCA assessments, equipercentile equating outperformed proportional scaling in development and validation cohorts. Propagating T-MoCA-MoCA-22 variability resulted in wider prediction intervals for T-MoCA-derived MoCA-30 estimates, indicating individual-level uncertainty, with intervals estimable only for T-MoCA scores ≥17 due to sparse data. At group level, T-MoCA is a valid remote measure of non-visual MoCA domains in iRBD and PD. The equating function supports cohort-level harmonization of MoCA-22 and MoCA-30 scores, while individual T-MoCA-derived MoCA-30 estimates should be interpreted with caution.

papers.title: The gut microbiota-derived butyrate improves gestational glucose homeostasis through HDAC3 inhibition and epigenetic activation of the SCGN/GLP-1 axis.
papers.abstract: A deficiency in the gut microbiota-derived metabolite butyrate is associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), yet the causative molecular pathways remain undefined. Given its established role as a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, we hypothesised that butyrate exerts its beneficial effects on gestational glucose homeostasis through epigenetic reprogramming of intestinal hormone secretion. We integrated clinical observation with causal experimentation. First, a nested case-control study measured serum butyrate and active GLP-1 in pregnant women. Second, a GDM mouse model induced by high-fat diet and antibiotics was treated with the butyrate-producing probiotic Clostridium butyricum for metabolic and microbial profiling. Colon tissues were analysed for HDAC expression and histone acetylation. Third, the mechanism was dissected in enteroendocrine cells using sodium butyrate, HDAC3 modulation, and integrated RNA-sequencing/H3K27ac chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing. Finally, HDAC3 heterozygous knockout mice were used for genetic validation. In the clinical cohort, serum butyrate and GLP-1 levels were consistently lower in women who developed GDM, evident both in early and mid-pregnancy (both p < 0.05). In mice, C. butyricum supplementation alleviated hyperglycaemia, insulin resistance, and circadian glucose rhythm disruption. This was paralleled by elevated systemic butyrate, enrichment of butyrate-producing gut bacteria, decreased colonic HDAC3 protein, and increased global histone H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac). Multi-omics analysis in enteroendocrine cells identified secretagogin (SCGN) as a direct target gene, with butyrate enhancing both its transcription and promoter-associated H3K27ac. Consequently, butyrate and HDAC3 knockdown increased SCGN expression and GLP-1 secretion, whereas HDAC3 overexpression suppressed this axis-an effect reversible by co-treatment with butyrate. The metabolic improvements and SCGN upregulation driven by C. butyricum were abolished in HDAC3-haploinsufficient mice. We demonstrate that butyrate ameliorates GDM by specifically inhibiting intestinal HDAC3. This inhibition epigenetically activates the transcription of SCGN via enhanced H3K27ac, leading to potentiated GLP-1 secretion. Our work delineates a novel gut microbiota-epigenetic-hormonal axis, identifying HDAC3 and the downstream SCGN/GLP-1 pathway as potential targets for the prevention or treatment of GDM.

papers.title: The dual use of traditional cigarettes and e-cigarettes and behavioral and psychological associated factors among Chinese adolescents.
papers.abstract: The dual use of traditional cigarettes and e-cigarettes is common among adolescents. Dual use is likely more harmful than smoking traditional cigarettes or using e-cigarettes alone. However, few studies have explored the behavioral and psychological factors associated with this pattern of tobacco use among Chinese adolescents. We surveyed high school students in all 31 provincial-level administrative divisions (PLADs) in mainland China. Tobacco use was categorized as current dual use, exclusive traditional cigarette use, exclusive e-cigarette use, and non-use. We collected 11 behavioral and psychological variables potentially associated with current tobacco use, including physical activity, screen time, sleep duration, diet, alcohol use, fighting, social self-control, self-esteem, self-efficacy, stress, and depression. Multinomial logistic regression adjusted for PLAD fixed effects was employed to analyze the associations. The weighted sample included 15,000 students with an equal distribution of sex and a median age of 17 years (IQR: 16-18). About 6.9% (95% confidence interval: 6.5%-7.3%) reported current dual use. Several behavioral and psychological factors, including excessive screen time (OR = 0.70, 95% CI = 0.61-0.80; appropriate screen time as the reference group), unhealthy dietary habits (OR = 1.34, 95% CI = 1.15-1.56; healthy diet as the reference group), alcohol use (occasional: OR = 5.53, 95% CI = 4.27-7.17; habitual: OR = 12.71, 95% CI = 9.24-17.47; never use as the reference group), fighting (occasionally: OR = 1.69, 95% CI = 1.41-2.03; habitual: OR = 1.83, 95% CI = 1.18-2.82; never fight as the reference group), strong social self-control (OR = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.57-0.82; moderate as the reference group), strong self-esteem (OR = 1.62, 95% CI = 1.36-1.94; moderate as the reference group), self-efficacy (strong: OR = 1.61, 95% CI = 1.38-1.88; weak: OR = 0.78, 95% CI = 0.62-0.97; moderate as the reference group), and strong stress (OR = 0.78, 95% CI = 0.64-0.95; moderate as the reference group), were found to be associated with the current dual use. Some of the above factors were also associated with the current exclusive use of traditional cigarettes or e-cigarettes. This study reports on the phenomenon of current dual use and its behavioral and psychological associated factors among high school students in China. Families and schools should pay attention to adolescents' health risk behaviors and psychological health, as these factors were found to be associated with tobacco use. Not applicable.

Effects of primary somatosensory cortex high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation combined with core stability training on pain and glutamate levels and neuromuscular function in chronic low back pain: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) involves pain-related changes in sensory processing, motor control, and broader neurobiological function. The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is a relevant neuromodulation target because it contributes to sensory-discriminative pain processing and exhibits maladaptive plasticity in chronic pain states. However, S1-targeted high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) has been insufficiently studied in CLBP. To determine whether S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training reduces pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP, and to explore associated changes in paraspinal muscle biomechanical properties, resting-state EEG activity, and serum metabolites. In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 36 adults with CLBP received active or sham S1 HD-tDCS combined with a standardized 4-week core stability training program. Pain-related scale was assessed using the VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ. Secondary outcomes included biomechanical properties of the lumbar erector spinae and multifidus measured using MyotonPRO. Exploratory outcomes included resting-state electroencephalographic alpha-band power spectral density (PSD) and phase-locking value (PLV) connectivity, as well as untargeted serum metabolomics in a subset of participants. Compared with sham stimulation, active S1 HD-tDCS was associated with greater reductions in VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ scores after treatment. The active group also showed larger decreases in lumbar erector spinae and multifidus tone and stiffness, along with greater improvement in elasticity. Resting-state EEG demonstrated increased alpha-band PSD across frontal, central, and parieto-occipital regions and reduced alpha-band PLV connectivity after active stimulation. In the metabolomics subset, active treatment was associated with greater reductions in circulating L-glutamate and enrichment of ferroptosis-related pathways. Changes in pain intensity were correlated with changes in paraspinal muscle stiffness, central alpha-band PSD, and L-glutamate levels. S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training may improve short-term pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP. The accompanying muscular, electrophysiological, and metabolomic findings were consistent with the clinical changes. These findings support S1-targeted HD-tDCS as a potential adjunct to exercise-based rehabilitation in CLBP. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300076620 (Registration date 2023-10-13).

papers.title: Differential circadian time modulates of dentate gyrus and CA1 excitation-inhibition balance and seizure threshold.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate seizure threshold and neuronal excitability in epilepsy. Temporal lobe seizures tend to arise more frequently during the diurnal phase relative to the nocturnal phase, yet dentate gyrus (DG) granule cells display elevated intrinsic excitability and CA1 pyramidal neurons show enhanced synaptic excitability at night. Here, we used male adult ICR mice (8-10 weeks old) as experimental subjects. Systemic pilocarpine injection was applied to pharmacologically trigger acute seizures, while AAV (pAAV2/9-CaMKIIα-hChR2 (H134R) - EYFP) delivery followed by optogenetic stimulation (10 Hz, 20 ms pulse width, 5 mW 473 nm blue light) was implemented to evoke region-specific hippocampal seizures. Combining continuous video-electroencephalography (vEEG) recording, optogenetically induced seizure assays, mRNA sequencing, and whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, we investigated circadian modulation of neuronal excitability and seizure threshold within the DG and CA1 subfields of the hippocampus. Our results revealed divergent circadian regulation of seizure thresholds between the DG and CA1 regions. Notably, the diurnal-nocturnal seizure threshold pattern in CA1 recapitulated that seen in systemic pilocarpien-provoked seizure models. We further confirmed that circadian cycles exert distinct regulatory effects on excitatory/inhibitory synaptic transmission and the intrinsic excitability of hippocampal principal neurons in the DG and CA1. Collectively, this work highlights region-specific circadian control over seizure susceptibility and the brain excitation-inhibition balance. Elucidating circadian influences on hippocampal physiology and seizure threshold will improve the translational value of anti-epileptic therapies and guide time-stratified seizure intervention strategies.

papers.title: Longitudinal relationship between sleep and emotional/behavioral problems in autism spectrum disorders: a cross-lagged panel analysis.
papers.abstract: Sleep, emotional, and behavioral problems are common comorbidities associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Current longitudinal research on the temporal links between sleep problems and emotional-behavioral problems shows inconsistent results among preschool children with ASD. Hence, this longitudinal study aimed to examine the temporal associations between emotional-behavioral and sleep problems among preschool children with ASD across two time points. Among 124 enrolled preschool children with ASD, 70 completed follow-up and constituted the final analytic sample (mean age 36.7 ± 10.2 months at T1). They were evaluated for developmental quotient using the Griffiths Development Scales-Chinese version (GDS-C), ASD symptoms using Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC) and Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), emotional and behavioral problems using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), and sleep problems using the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) at time 1 (T1). The evaluations were replicated at a follow-up appointment 18 months after T1 (time 2; T2). The cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) was employed to examine the potential relationship between CBCL and CSHQ scores in the children. The total CBCL score at T1 could predict the CSHQ at T2 (β = 0.348, t = 3.105, p = 0.002), whereas the CSHQ at T1 could not predict the CBCL at T2 (β = 0.117, t = 1.083, p = 0.279). Findings remained robust across five sensitivity subsets after excluding subgroups with distinct rehabilitation exposure, younger age, higher development quotients, girls, or mild ASD symptoms. Emotional-behavioral problems predict sleep problems 18 months later in preschool ASD children. Screening of these symptoms during follow-up supports early sleep-risk monitoring. • Sleep, emotional, and behavioral problems are common comorbidities associated with ASD. • Thus, researching their temporal correlation over time is necessary. • Emotional and behavioral problems indicate a positive temporal correlation at T1, which was also evident for sleep problems at T2, in children with ASD. • Emotional and behavioral problems in preschool children with ASD can forecast sleep problems that develop 18 months later, providing guidance for clinical decision-making.

papers.title: AnySleep: a channel-agnostic deep learning system for high-resolution sleep staging in multi-center cohorts.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, yet studying its dynamics requires manual sleep staging, a labor-intensive step in research and clinical care. Across centers, polysomnography (PSG) recordings are traditionally scored in 30-s epochs for pragmatic, not physiological, reasons and vary in electrode count, montage, and subject characteristics. These constraints challenge harmonized multi-center studies and the discovery of robust biomarkers on shorter timescales. We present AnySleep, a deep neural network that scores sleep from any electroencephalography (EEG) or electrooculography (EOG) data at adjustable temporal resolutions. We trained and validated the model on over 20,000 overnight recordings (>200,000 h of EEG and EOG) from 28 datasets across multiple clinics to promote robust generalization across sites. The model attains state-of-the-art performance and surpasses or equals established baselines at 30-s epochs. Performance improves with more channels, yet remains strong when EOG is absent, or only EOG or single EEG derivations (frontal, central, or occipital) are available. On sub-30-s timescales, the model captures short wake intrusions consistent with arousals and improves the prediction of pathophysiological conditions (obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy type 1, insomnia) over 30-s scoring. We make the model publicly available to facilitate large-scale studies with heterogeneous electrode setups and accelerate biomarker discovery in sleep.

papers.title: Cre-loxP as an option in cardiovascular disease research.
papers.abstract: The Cre-LoxP system is based on site-specific recombination mediated by the enzyme Cre recombinase. This system allows spatiotemporal control of gene expression in inducible models by utilizing specific promoters or enhancers that direct the expression of Cre recombinase in particular tissues or as a response to external signals at a specific moment in the life of the model organism, such as drug administration. In cardiovascular research, the Cre-LoxP system has been fundamental in generating mouse models replicating specific human pathological conditions. A growing area of interest is the use of Cre-LoxP in optogenetics, where it allows the expression of light-sensitive ion channels to modulate the activity of specific tissues such as the heart. This approach provides new avenues for studying cardiac electrophysiology and developing targeted therapeutic strategies.
